title: The first night
text: The door closes at nine. The light in the ceiling does not go out. Somewhere along the landing a man is singing very softly, and another is telling him to stop.

outcomes.text: I lay on my back with my eyes on the ceiling and learned the building from its noises: the pipes, the key-ring, the long tide of voices. By dawn I could tell the officers apart by their footsteps.

intel: The night officer does his round at ten past and again at four

outcomes.text: I listened, and what I heard was a boy two cells down crying into a blanket. I heard it for a week. I never mentioned it to anyone, and neither did he.
{c.first} looked me over for a while, and then moved a box off my bunk. 'Top or bottom,' he said, 'doesn't matter, you'll be here a while.' We were civil from that moment.
{c.first} said nothing at all, for most of the night. In the morning he said two words, and they were 'toilet etiquette', and a very detailed list followed.

choices.label: Write a letter you won't send

outcomes.text: I wrote four pages to my mother, then burned them in the sink with a match I'd been given. It wasn't brave. It was the only door I had.
I wrote to the person I'd done it to. I put no address on it, because I didn't have one, and folded it small. It's still in the Bible I was given.

title: The man on the top bunk
text: {c.first} has a way of doing things in the cell. He does them in a set order, at a set time, and he does not like it when they change. Today I changed one.

outcomes.text: He took it with a nod. By the end of the month I knew his ritual better than my own, and we had a rhythm that made a seven-by-ten box feel almost like a room.
He told me about the habits of a man who'd done twelve years already. It was the best education I got in that building.

intel: How the old hands read a new officer

outcomes.text: There was a silence, then a long look. He moved one thing back, and we both pretended it hadn't happened.
It escalated. A shove, a raised voice, an officer at the door. Both of us got a write-up and neither of us got an apology.
The request went in, and an officer read it and tore it in half. I stayed. In the end, I was glad.
A move, to a cell with a man who sang all night. I'd have given a great deal for the first one back.

title: Whose table
text: The mess hall has a geography. There are tables for the gangs, tables for the old hands, a table for the ones who talk to the staff. There's one empty seat, and I'm holding a tray.

outcomes.text: It was the table of the Quiet Men. They did not look up. They did not move their trays. At the end of the meal, one of them, without looking at me, said, 'Tomorrow the other end.'
It was the wrong seat. I knew it as soon as I'd sat, from the quality of the silence. A man at the end got up and I was moved, by a hand on my shoulder, to the floor.
I ate quickly, at the end of the counter, and left. Nobody objected. Nobody noticed. For a few weeks I was a tray and a pair of hands.
A kitchen worker slid an extra piece of bread across the counter without looking at me. I took it. I did not know why, and I didn't ask.
I asked an older man who was sitting on his own. He looked at my shoes for a long while and said, 'Next to me. Don't talk.' I didn't. We've been in the same row for years.
I asked a younger man, who happened to be a member of the Brickhouse Boys. He was delighted to tell me everything, in exchange for something I didn't understand until it was too late.

title: The test
text: It's the third week. I'm walking back from the library when a man steps into the corridor and doesn't step out. 'You got a light?' It's a question with a price.

outcomes.text: He took it, nodded, and let me through. Everyone in the corridor watched. By lunchtime I had a reputation as someone who could be talked to. By dinner, as someone who could be talked into things.
He lit up, looked at the match, and said, 'Fair.' It cost me a pack in the end, but I was left alone for a good while.
It took about four seconds to go wrong. I held my ground, and got hit for it, and hit back. It was over before an officer came, and I had a story that preceded me.
He looked at me, decided I was not worth the paperwork, and let me by. I walked the rest of the way with a shaking hand.

choices.label: Turn round and go the long way

outcomes.text: The long way took ten minutes. Everyone had seen it. A man in the library asked me if I was all right, in a voice that meant 'you're going to have a hard time'.
I walked the long way for six months. It's a good corridor. Nothing ever happened in it.

title: An offer
text: Two men are waiting in my cell when I come back from the yard. One sits on my bunk. 'We've been asking about you,' he says. 'We think you'd do well with some friends.'

outcomes.text: It was done with a handshake and a piece of paper I never saw. The next week, a man who'd been leaning on me crossed the yard to avoid me. I belonged to someone, and everyone knew it.
The Congregation took me in, with the soft menace of a church that knows where you live. I got prayer, a place at the table and a list of favours to be done.
'Think about it,' he said, and left a pack of cigarettes on the bunk. It sat there for a week. I did not touch it, and it stayed there.
They took it well, which was worse. A few days later the man in the next cell was suddenly very interested in my commissary.
I told them I'd think. I thought for months. They watched, and waited. It was the nearest thing I'd had to a position in the whole place.

intel: Who actually runs the east landing

outcomes.text: I told them I'd see. They said, 'Of course', in a voice that made it clear I'd said something stupid.

title: What you owe
text: It started with a pack of cigarettes and a game of cards. It is now eleven packs, the interest, and a man called {i.first} who stands next to me in the queue and says my name pleasantly.

outcomes.text: It took everything I had and some things I hadn't. {i.first} counted it, nodded, and said it was a pleasure doing business. I slept for the first time in a week.
I paid it by borrowing from someone else, and from there it never ended. But the moment I'd paid {i.first}, I felt a weight come off.
I said I'd have it on Friday. And then the next Friday. He smiled the whole time. On the fourth Friday he stopped smiling.
I got three weeks. In three weeks I found a way of getting a thing from outside that paid it off. I shouldn't have done it, but it worked.
The officer listened to the whole thing and then wrote a name in a book. The man vanished to another wing. I was left alone and marked as someone who talks.
The officer shrugged, and said he'd see what he could do. The next day I was moved to a different landing. The debt came with me.

title: The shower block
text: The shower block is the one place with no cameras. It is also the only place with hot water, and the water is on for four minutes. Today there are two men by the door.

outcomes.text: They watched me go past. Four minutes of hot water, under a ceiling and a feeling. Nothing happened. Nothing happens, mostly, and that is the trick of it.
I got in and I got hurt. It was quick. They knew what they were doing. I was found by an orderly, and I told him I'd slipped.
I waited. I waited until I had nearly missed it, and went in with the last men. Cold water, quick and safe.
I waited, and for a month I washed at the sink. It isn't dignity. It's a policy.
I asked the man in the next cell. He said yes at once. Nobody touched us. Having a friend, however slight, is a form of armour.
I asked, and he said no, and I went in on my own. I made it. I owe nobody anything, and it feels both ways.

title: In the kitchen
text: The kitchen is the best job in the building and the most dangerous. There are knives, which are counted, and a loading bay, which is not. Today a man from the other side of the hatch asks me for a favour.

outcomes.text: It was small and in a cloth, and I didn't look. {off.first}, the officer, saw it and looked at the wall. I was given a bit of rank, and a reason to lie awake.
It was a phone. I knew when I felt the weight. The man said, 'Thursday', and I knew that someone was going to ask me again.
He nodded, and went. In the morning there was salt in the porridge, and in the afternoon, in the bread. It would be a long month.
He took it well and stopped asking. But in the queue, afterwards, there were a few more hard looks than usual.
He thanked me, and the man was gone by the end of the week. I got a better shift, and, for the rest of the sentence, a very short list of friends.
The supervisor looked at me for a very long time. 'You'd better be right,' he said. I was, and it cost me.

title: The law library
text: The law books are kept in a locked bay at the back, in a separate room, and you can sign up for an hour. Most people use it to look up other people. Today a man is sitting in the other chair, reading my case.

outcomes.text: He was a jailhouse lawyer with a broken nose and a flair for procedure. He'd noticed a deadline I'd missed and a form I'd never been given. In two hours he gave me more than my own lawyer had in four years.

intel: A missed disclosure in the original trial

outcomes.text: He was a con, and I realised too late. I'd handed him details he could sell, to a man in the next wing, for a pack of cigarettes.
I closed it and left. It was a trap, or it wasn't. In prison you're not allowed to know.
I left and came back later, at a time I knew he wouldn't be there. I read in peace.
He said it would cost me. He said it would cost me a packet of coffee a month, which was a lot of coffee. But he knew where the documents were.
He said no. He said he was already doing four cases, and had a real lawyer's disdain for the ones who'd been in the dark. But he gave me the forms.

title: The chapel door
text: The chaplain has been leaving the chapel door open at the same time every Thursday for a year. He doesn't ask anyone to come in. Tonight I'm outside it, deciding.

outcomes.text: It smelled of floor polish and candle smoke. Eight of us on plastic chairs. The chaplain said nothing about God for a long time. He asked what we were afraid of. I told him.
I went in for the warmth and stayed for the singing. I can't sing. The man next to me couldn't either, and it didn't matter.
I stood in the corridor with my back against the wall and listened to a hymn I didn't know. Nobody saw me. It was a good ten minutes.
I stayed outside. The chaplain nodded when he came out, and said, 'Same time next week.' There's a lot to be said for patient men.

choices.label: Use the room for something else

outcomes.text: The chapel is the one place nobody searches. I used it for a handover that ought not to have happened in a holy place. I felt bad about it for a long time.
I used the chapel to speak to a man I couldn't speak to anywhere else. We sat in the back row and talked, like worshippers.

intel: A bent officer on the east landing

title: A drawing
text: An envelope with a children's drawing in it: a house, a very large sun, a figure standing in the garden with enormous hands. Underneath, in careful pencil: DADDY / MUMMY. I don't know which one the child meant.

choices.label: Pin it up above the bunk

outcomes.text: It's been there since. The officers do their searches around it. The cellmate once moved a thing, and then moved it back. We have never discussed it.
I pinned it up and the corners peeled, and I put it up again with toothpaste. It lasted for years, in the end.
It took me a week. I drew a picture, badly, of the garden. A reply came with a drawing of mine, much improved. We've been corresponding for years, in the language of the very young.
I wrote four pages, and tore them up, and wrote one. The one is the best thing I have ever written.

choices.label: Put it away, and don't look at it

outcomes.text: I put it in the bottom of the box, where I would not see it. I needed to survive the day, and that was not a day for pictures.
I looked at it once, put it away, and didn't write. There are things that you can't look at until you can.

title: The glass
text: The visiting room has a table, a clock and a pane of scratched Perspex. {off.first} the officer stands by the door. On the other side of the glass is the person I've been waiting for since the last time.

outcomes.text: I said it all. I said it badly. They listened and nodded and said a very simple sentence back that undid the rehearsal. We both cried, and the officer looked at the ceiling.
I said it. It was the wrong way round, and somehow they heard the right thing. 'I know,' they said. It was enough.
We talked about the weather, and the dog, and the price of tea. The clock ran down. I'd never loved anyone so much as in that talk about the price of tea.
We talked about nothing, and it was the right thing. At the end, they put their hand on the glass and I put mine on it.

choices.label: Tell them not to come any more

outcomes.text: I said it as kindly as I could. I said it was for their sake. They looked at me for a very long moment and said, 'No.' I didn't know whether to be relieved.
I said it, and they believed it. They stopped coming. I told myself it was a gift. It took a long time to stop believing that.

title: A game on the landing
text: A game of cards has started on the third landing, and the stakes are not cigarettes. They are favours. Someone has just put down a name.

outcomes.text: I played the hand I had, which was the right hand. I won a favour from a man who couldn't afford to lose it. It's a currency I've been spending ever since.

intel: A debt that someone cannot pay

outcomes.text: I lost the hand and a name, a favour on the books for a man who would need it. I paid it, in time, in a way I won't go into.
I stayed on the rail, and watched, and counted. A man who watches long enough knows who cheats.

intel: The man who deals twice from the bottom

outcomes.text: I watched for an hour and left. Nobody invited me back. It was both a loss and a decision.
It was a snitch's move, and no one saw it. The game stopped for a month, and I was not the only one who suspected a rat.
I told an officer. He nodded and said he knew. I was left with the hot, small taste of having done something and not having helped.

title: Ink
text: There's a man on the second landing who does tattoos with a needle from a motor and ink from a melted comb. His chair is a plastic bucket. He has a queue.

outcomes.text: It took three hours and hurt like hell. The name on my forearm is my daughter's. Hers is the first name I've had written on me. I look at it when the day goes bad.
It was the name of the block, the gang and a date. It's a bid for belonging. It's on my arm for life, and so is the price.

choices.label: Offer to help run the queue

outcomes.text: I held the lookout and counted the minutes. In the end I got a cut of the tobacco and a story to tell. The inked ones remembered who stood watch.
We were caught on the third day. The man took the blame and I took a lesser one. Both of us lost a few privileges.
I stayed out. The queue went on without me. The man had to move his chair twice.
I stayed out. A month later, the whole landing was searched, and the chair was found in the third cell along. I had a clean sheet.

title: Something on the roof
text: At two in the morning a small shape crosses the beam of the floodlight and lands on the roof of the workshop. In the morning a man in the yard asks if I saw anything.

outcomes.text: He nodded, and a week later I found a packet of tobacco under my pillow. I hadn't asked for it. That's how you know you're in.
He grinned and said, 'Good.' I didn't know what I'd agreed to, but I knew that I'd agreed.
The roof was searched, and a package was found. The officer wrote my name in a book and under it, a tick. I don't know what the tick means.
I told {off.first}. He nodded, and made a note. The following week, I was given a job in the library.
It took two men and a ladder. In the bag there were four phones and a lot of small, expensive pills. I took one phone and left the rest. A man who takes everything gets caught.

intel: A route up to the workshop roof

outcomes.text: I got as far as the ledge, and the floodlight swung. I froze for a very long minute. Then it moved on, and I went back down with nothing.

title: She stopped returning calls
text: My lawyer hasn't answered in five months. Today a letter arrives from her office on thin cream paper. It uses the word 'regrettably' twice.

outcomes.text: I wrote eleven letters, all polite. One reached her. She took the case back, grudgingly, with a few ground rules. It's a poor marriage but it's a marriage.
I wrote to her firm, to the bar association and to her mother, who sent back a kind, evasive postcard. She stayed on.
I did it. I did it in the library at night with a dictionary and a sheaf of forms. I got a hearing, and the judge remarked on the quality of the drafting. It didn't help the case, but it helped me.
I did it and got buried by the procedure. The judge was kind. The state's lawyer was not. I learned more about the law in a month than I had in the previous ten years.
A pro bono clinic took the file. It was an eager twenty-six-year-old with a law degree and a conscience. I asked her how many she'd saved. 'None,' she said. 'Yet.'
There was nobody. The waiting lists were years. I put my name on three of them.

title: The test
text: A student at the innocence clinic has found an unopened evidence box. Inside is a stain the lab never tested, and a signature on the chain-of-custody form that does not match.

choices.label: Ask for the test, and wait

outcomes.text: It took fourteen months. The result came back on a Tuesday: not mine. A second profile, no match on the database, and a hearing date. I had to sit down on the floor.
The lab was backlogged. The test was done at last. It was inconclusive, a stain too degraded to read. It was the worst news I could imagine and, somehow, it kept the case open.
A news programme ran it. The prosecutor made a statement. The pressure moved the hearing forward by half a year, but it also moved a lot of people's minds against me.
A journalist wrote a long piece. It was fair and generous. I was told it had been read in the prosecutor's office with a sense of professional alarm.

choices.label: Do nothing; be afraid of it

outcomes.text: I let the student do all the work. I could not bear to get my hopes up again. When the box was opened I was on the yard, pretending it was a day like any other.
I told the clinic to stop. I said it wasn't worth another heartbreak. They didn't stop. I was furious, and they were right.

title: A letter from the family
text: A letter has come through the victims' liaison office. It's addressed to me, and it is handwritten, and the handwriting is a woman's.

outcomes.text: It said that she hadn't forgiven me and wasn't going to. It said her son was eleven when it happened and was nineteen now. It said that she wanted me to know that a person had been lost. I read it once, and I have never forgotten a word.
I read it in the chapel. She wrote about her husband's hands. I wrote back. It took me months. I don't know if she read it.
I put it in my box, unopened, with the others. Eventually there were five.
I gave it to the chaplain to hold. He said he'd keep it until I wanted it. He kept it for twelve years.
I said I was sorry, in the plainest words I could find. I said there wasn't anything I could do. I did not ask for anything. No answer came.
I wrote four lines. She replied with two. It was the beginning of a long, painful correspondence, and the most honest thing in my sentence.

title: A deal
text: A man in a good coat is sitting in the interview room with a folder. He says that I am someone who knows things, and that there is a way of using them. He says 'cooperation', slowly, as if it were an old friend.

outcomes.text: The offer was a reduced sentence and a transfer. All I had to do was say what I knew about a man called {i.first}. It was nothing I hadn't already guessed. I thought about it for a month.

intel: The prosecutors want a name on the east landing

outcomes.text: He wanted a statement about a murder I knew a little about. He wanted my name on it. I left with a copy of the offer and a feeling I would carry like a stone.
I signed. I did it in a room with a window. Six months later I was gone, to another prison, with three years off. There wasn't a person in the building who didn't know why.
I took it. The man I named got fifteen years. I never saw him again, but I thought about him daily.
I said no. He didn't argue. He packed his folder and said, 'That's what they all say, the first time.' It was another four years before I saw anyone in a good coat.
I said no, and said it loudly, in a corridor where others could hear it. It cost me nothing and bought me a great deal.

title: The old head
text: He has been inside since before I could drive. He sits on the same bench every day and does the crossword in pencil. He has not said a word to me in two years. Today he says, 'Sit down.'

outcomes.text: He taught me for an hour: who to be careful of, what to eat, how to hold my face. 'The thing about time,' he said, 'is you don't do it. It does you. Be doing something.' I've never forgotten that.
He told me a story about a man he'd known who'd lost his mind in the fourth year. He said, 'Don't be that man.' I said I wouldn't.

intel: What the old heads say about the new warden

outcomes.text: He nodded, and went back to the crossword. I never got another invitation.
I told him I was busy. He smiled. 'Yes,' he said. 'You are.' It is the thing I regret most from the second year.
'Nothing,' he said. 'That's the point.' It took me a long time to understand it.
He wanted a favour, small, from the library. I did it. We were friends after that, if that's what you call an old man and a young one with a pencil between them.

title: The kid on the landing
text: He is nineteen and he looks fifteen. He has been in for a week and he hasn't eaten. Someone has already spoken to him about the debt that he is going to owe.

outcomes.text: I taught him the order of things. I stood next to him in the mess hall, and nobody touched him. He called me 'sir' for a month. He was released four years later, and the first letter I received was from him.
I took him on. It cost me. A debt of his became a debt of mine, and I didn't tell him. He's out now, and doing well. I'd do it again.
I kept out of it. In a month he'd found someone else's wing. I did not see him again, and I know what that means.
I looked away. It's a decision with a long half-life.
A boy who owes you is a pair of hands. He took parcels, kept watch, did what I asked. He thought I was kind. I'm not proud of it.
I used him, in a small way. Nobody was hurt. But I saw his face when he realised what he had been, and I will not forget it.

title: Someone who calls you by name
text: {off.first} has called me by name for six months. Not my number. My name. This morning at the cell door he said, 'Mind how you go, {off.first}'s not on tonight,' as though he were warning me about the weather.

outcomes.text: I told him about my daughter. He told me about his. It's the nearest thing to a friendship that the building permits, and it's not much, and it's a great deal.

intel: His shift pattern changes on the first of the month

outcomes.text: I told him one thing, and he told me one thing back. It was enough. It's amazing how little it takes.
In my experience, kindness is a form of leverage. I stayed civil, and gave nothing. He seemed to understand that. We nodded at each other for years.
I answered in monosyllables. He seemed hurt, and then, finally, bored. I felt both relief and loss.
I asked for a book to be let in. A week later it came, with a note that said 'Don't make me regret it.' I haven't.
I asked him to look the other way once. He did. A year later he asked me to look the other way. I haven't forgotten it.

title: Not a good one
text: {off.first} is the kind of officer the building keeps. He finds a reason for a search, a delay, a cold meal, and then a reason to write it down. Today he has stopped at my cell with a clipboard and a smile.

outcomes.text: It was a long afternoon, and a longer evening, and a night I didn't sleep. When he'd gone, I picked up the pieces and put them back. I told nobody.
I stood against the wall and took it. It's a form of dignity. He wrote nothing down, in the end, and I'm still not sure why.
I said something. It was exactly the right thing, and it was exactly the wrong thing, and the charge sheet that followed listed it as 'insolence'.
I answered back. The other prisoners had been waiting years for someone to. I got three days' segregation and a month of cold stares from the staff, and an inch of grudging respect from the wing.
A form, a number, a stamp. It went through channels. A man in a suit came to ask me questions. {off.first} was moved to another wing. I wasn't thanked.
The complaint was lost. The next month, I was moved to a worse cell. These two facts may or may not be connected.

title: A stranger's letters
text: A woman I've never met has written to me. She says she saw my name on a list at her church. Her handwriting is very upright, and she asks no questions about what I did.

outcomes.text: We wrote for six years. She never asked what I did. She sent photographs of her garden. When I got out, I found it exactly as she'd described it.
I wrote back, and the correspondence grew. She sent a book each month. The books were the kind that change how a person thinks, and I'm grateful.
I held the letter for a month. Then I wrote, awkwardly, and she answered at once, as if no time had passed.
I waited, and waited, and in the end it was too late. A second letter came, and then no third. I don't know why I didn't answer.
I did the checks: the name, the church, the address. Everything was real. I wrote, and apologised for the delay. She answered in two lines: 'I'd have done the same.'
I suspected a con. I was right: it was a scheme, a request for a loan, and a moment of real disappointment. I had thought it was kindness.

title: The first day
text: {sup.first}, your sergeant, hands you a ring of keys and a radio, and says the same sentence he says to every recruit: 'Nobody knows. Not me. Not the warden. You'll learn it faster if you stop pretending you do.'

outcomes.text: I shadowed him all week. He did a hundred small things without seeming to think about them: the tilt of a head, a half step to the left. By Friday I could recognise the shape of a bad afternoon before it happened.
I wrote everything down in a notebook I kept in my sock. It was an odd thing to do, and I still have it. The things I wrote on the first day are the things that matter most.
I walked down the middle of the landing as if I owned it. A man said something about my boots. I smiled at him. I'd done everything right in the wrong order.
I walked the landing at a deliberate pace. The wing watched. A man at the end nodded, once, in a way that said he'd decided something about me.
I did my job and said nothing. By the end of the first month, no one on the wing could tell you my name. This is its own kind of failure, and its own kind of safety.
I kept my head down and my radio on. It was slow, safe and entirely forgettable. For a first year, that's no bad thing.

title: The rules nobody wrote
text: {co.first}, who has done fourteen years, takes you aside after your third week. 'There are two sets of rules in here,' {co.he} says. 'The ones in the book and the ones that keep you alive. Want to hear the second set?'

outcomes.text: {co.first} taught me: who to talk to, who to leave alone, how to stand in a doorway so a man can see your hands. Some of it was wisdom and some of it was habit that had calcified, and I couldn't always tell which.
It was a list. Don't take food from the inmates. Don't tell anyone where you live. Never be the last officer on a landing. Never be alone with one of them if you can help it. I've kept all four.

choices.label: Say you'll go by the book

outcomes.text: {co.first} looked at me for a moment, and nodded. 'Good,' {co.he} said, 'and when you find out the book isn't enough, come and find me.' I did, about six weeks later.
I said I'd stick to the book. {co.first} said nothing, but I saw a look. By the end of the year I knew what it meant.
{co.first} laughed. 'There's always a catch,' {co.he} said. 'The catch is that you start using the second set for yourself.' I wrote that down.
{co.first} said, 'You'll do.' It was the most generous thing anyone had said to me that month.

title: The first one
text: At 4.50 in the morning, on a routine check, I find a man on the floor of cell nineteen. He's cold. His face is calm. The alarm goes up, and I do everything I was trained to do, and none of it matters.

outcomes.text: I did the checks, I called the code, I started compressions and kept going until the nurse touched my arm. The report was clean. The sound of the ribs is not in the report.
The book saved me, as it does. I followed every step. The coroner found no fault. I found a great deal.
I got through the shift. I went to the car park, sat in the front seat, and shook for twenty minutes. Nobody came. Nobody does.
I wept in the locker room. {sup.first} found me there, sat next to me, said nothing for a minute, and then told me about his first one. I've never felt less alone.
The service offered a counsellor, a tired man in a small room, with a box of tissues and a clock. He listened. It helped, a little, and I went back more than I expected to.
I asked for a day off and got a form. By the time it was approved I'd done another three shifts. Nothing came of it, but I filed it.

title: The cell extraction
text: A man in cell twelve has barricaded the door with his mattress and a bed frame. He says he has a blade. The shift supervisor wants the extraction team. You are the newest on it.

choices.label: Go in first, by the book

outcomes.text: We went in as trained. Shield, bar, shield, bar. It took four minutes. He was uninjured and the officers were uninjured and the report says that everyone did as they were told. That's the nearest thing to a good day there is.
I went in first. The blade was real, and a small one. A hand struck my arm, a quick flash, a lot of noise. I came out with a gash and a medal of sorts.
I stayed on the second line. It was the safe position and nobody commented. Later, I found I had not been picked for the next team.
I let the others go in. Afterwards nobody said anything about it, which was worse than if they had.
I spoke to him through the hatch, for forty minutes. I said his name, which I'd learned from the file. He came out at last with the blade held loosely. It was a terrible, tiring kind of triumph.
I tried, and he talked back, and for a few minutes it worked. Then he heard the shields in the corridor and everything broke. It ended the way the other way would have, only longer.

title: A fight on the landing
text: Two inmates are on the floor, one on top, hitting hard. The one underneath has stopped moving. I am the nearest officer and my radio is already shouting.

choices.label: Wade in with all the force I have

outcomes.text: I got between them in two steps and put the man on top onto the floor face-down. It took a lot of force. It took more than I had a right to. The report called it 'proportionate'. I am the only one who knows.
I put him down, hard, with a knee in the back. The medics said afterwards that it was necessary, and I said it was. I looked at my hands later.

choices.label: Use the minimum, and wait for backup

outcomes.text: I used the baton as a barrier, and my voice, and a hand on the man's collar. It took ninety seconds and it was ugly. The man on the floor lived. The report was long and clean.
I got between them. I took a punch for it. When the others arrived, it was over, and I had a split lip and a good report.
I waited. I know that 'wait' is in the book. It was eleven seconds. When I looked at the man on the floor afterwards, I counted them again.
I stood at the rail and waited for the response team. By the time they arrived, it was too late for the man underneath. The inquiry cleared me. I didn't feel cleared.

title: The inquiry
text: A man from Internal Affairs sits across the table in the small interview room. He has a tape recorder, a notebook and my incident report from March, which he turns to face me.

choices.label: Tell it exactly as it was

outcomes.text: I said what I did and why I did it, and where I thought I'd gone too far. He wrote it down without comment. Nothing came of it that year. I think he found it unusual to hear it said.
I told him all of it. The union rep winced. I was given a written warning, which is the lightest thing they have. I slept better than I had in months.
I stuck to it, word for word, and he kept looking at me. In the end he closed the notebook. 'Thank you,' he said. I knew he knew. I knew I knew.
I said what the report said. He asked if I wanted to add anything. I said no. It was true, and it was not the truth, and it cost me.
The union rep spoke for me for most of the hour. He's very good at it. The matter was closed 'without findings', and I owed him a drink and a great deal more.
The rep sat beside me and said 'no comment' on my behalf nine times. It worked. I never got over how easy it was.

title: A small favour
text: An inmate I've known for two years catches my eye in the corridor. 'Boss,' he says, 'would you ring my sister and tell her I'm all right? She worries.' He gives me a number on a scrap of paper.

outcomes.text: It was a thirty-second call to a woman in a kitchen. She cried. I said, 'He's fine, he's eating,' and hung up. It was a breach of three separate rules, and it was the best thing I did that week.
I made the call. She said thank you eleven times. A week later the inmate stopped me and said something quiet, and I realised I had acquired a friend and a debt.
I told him I couldn't. I told him why. He nodded, and said, 'Fair.' Two weeks later he warned me about a thing that was going to kick off on the east landing. I think he'd respected that I said no.

intel: Something is being arranged on the east landing

outcomes.text: I said no, and meant it. He didn't ask again. But I thought about the sister, in the kitchen, for a long time.
I wrote it up. By the book. It was the right thing to do, and I felt like a bastard. He was moved to a different wing a month later, and nobody told me why.
I reported it. The supervisor thanked me and made a face. 'You'll get a name for that,' he said, and I did.

title: An envelope
text: It's on the passenger seat of my car. It wasn't there when I parked. No note. There's $800 in it, and a Post-it with the name of an inmate, a landing and a word: 'Thursday'.

choices.label: Take it, and do what it asks

outcomes.text: Thursday came. I looked at the wall for eleven minutes. Something went through a hatch. The next week, there was a second envelope. I have never been more afraid and more relieved.
I took it and did it. I told myself it was one time. By October it was a regular arrangement, and by Christmas I had a second set of keys in my head.
I left it on the seat and drove home. The next morning it was gone. Nobody said anything. For a week, I looked at every inmate I walked past.
I left it, and drove to the station, and sat in the car park for a quarter of an hour. Then I went in and did my shift. Nothing happened. That was worse.

I took it to my sergeant. He looked at it for a long time and then at me. 'Good,' he said. The inmate was transferred, and I had a month of cold shoulders from the wing. It's the best decision I made that year.

intel: A trafficking route into the east wing

outcomes.text: I took it to Internal Affairs. A man named {sup.first} sent me for coffee while he made calls. I was given a recommendation and a list of enemies.

intel: A trafficking route into the east wing

title: The staff who aren't
text: {co.first} has been buying rounds for three months with notes I haven't seen before. Tonight {co.he} says, 'There's something you ought to be in on.'

outcomes.text: It was a small ring: four officers, a trusted trade-in of phones and tobacco, a share for everyone. The money was real. The way it was explained made it sound like a pension plan.
I listened, and said I'd think. For a month, I was both outsider and insider. At the end of it I had a hard choice and no easy way out.

intel: A ring of four officers on the east landing

outcomes.text: I said no. {co.first} nodded, and said nothing more. The following week my locker was moved. The week after that, someone put a dead rat in it. I was never invited again.

intel: A ring of four officers on the east landing

outcomes.text: I said no and walked away. The silence in the canteen the next day was a physical thing. I ate my sandwich in the car.
I took notes for two weeks and handed them to a woman in a grey suit. Eight months later the ring was dismantled. I was never named. Everyone knew.
I told IA. They asked me to wear a wire. I did. I'll say no more. I'd do it again, and I'd never do it twice.

title: Too much attention
text: An inmate who has been on the wing for three years has begun leaving his work station to talk to you. He's clever, and kind, and I find that I am listening for the sound of his voice.

outcomes.text: I told him I couldn't talk to him except about the job. He said, 'I understand,' and, to his credit, did. The rest of the year was a lot quieter and a lot colder.
I had myself moved to another landing. A month later I had a note, handwritten, from him, saying thank you. I never learned what for.
I told my sergeant. He looked at me for a while. 'Thank you,' he said. 'That's the bravest thing you'll do this year.' I was reassigned.
I walked into the deputy's office and said it. The deputy said nothing for a minute, and then helped me do what had to be done. It was the best bit of management I ever saw.
It was a year. It was a long, strained, secret year, and it ended in a shared look across a corridor and the smell of floor polish. He was transferred. I was found out.
I let it go on, and I paid for it for years. I'd do almost anything to get one more hour of that, and it was the worst thing I've done.

title: Short-staffed
text: Three officers are off sick and another two are on leave. The roster has a hole in it that the supervisor is trying to fill with names. He's looking at me.

outcomes.text: Sixteen hours. The wing is different at four in the morning: quieter, closer. I made a rule of walking the whole of it twice. I got home at six and fell asleep in the car.
I took it. It was my fourth that month. My wife said nothing at all when I got home, which she says only when she's furious.
I said I couldn't. He nodded, and said, 'No problem', in a voice that said there was. Someone else took the shift. It was the right decision, and a small, hard one.
I said I'd promised my daughter. He made a face and wrote something. I got the weekend, and she got a father.
I called a meeting, and fifty officers came. It became a letter, and then a bulletin, and then a headline. I was not popular upstairs.
I wrote to the union rep. He wrote to the warden. The warden wrote to the minister. In the end we got four more officers, none of whom had been trained.

title: The board
text: The promotion board is three people at a table and a flipchart. They have read your record, your reports and the comments of the officers who work with you. One of them asks, 'What is the hardest decision you've made in this job?'

choices.label: Tell the truth about a mistake

outcomes.text: I told them about the landing in March. I told them what I'd have done differently. They looked at each other. The chair said, 'That's the right answer', and wrote something down.
I told them I'd made a mistake. I'd assumed it would cost me, and instead it won me their trust. That's the most surprising thing I've found about authority.
I told the story of the hostage, and the radio, and the chaplain. It's a good story. It was the right one for a promotion board. I was promoted within the month.
I told them what I'd done well. It was true. It was also what everybody tells a board, and the chair's face betrayed no surprise.
I said that no decision in this job is only one decision. They liked that, in a way. They liked it less in the notes.
I said that. It was true. I did not get the promotion that year, and the one who did was a man who'd answered the question.

title: The inspectors
text: A delegation from the ministry arrives with clipboards. The warden has told all staff to be on their best behaviour. The wing has been cleaned in the night. Nobody has told the inmates what's happening, but they know.

outcomes.text: I did exactly what was asked. I said the right things, in the right order, to the right people. The report was glowing, and utterly false.
I followed the script. Inspectors look for what they've been told to look for, and we gave it to them. It's an art, and I had learned it.
I stopped one of them in a corridor. I told her about the staffing, the broken locks on the east landing, the ratio. She wrote it down. A year later, there were eight more officers.
I told the truth. It cost me a year of good evaluations. It bought four months of better staffing, and it was worth it.

choices.label: Make sure an inmate gets heard

outcomes.text: I made sure the inspector's route went past cell thirty. A man there handed her a letter. It was a good letter. He was moved to another wing the next week, and I never learned how he got on.
I steered her to a man with a long list of complaints, all legitimate. He told her everything. I spent a month defending myself, and I'd do it again.

title: The memo
text: A memo has been pinned to the staff-room noticeboard. It uses the words 'efficiencies' and 'rationalisation'. By lunch, everybody has worked out that it means fewer officers and more inmates.

outcomes.text: I was one of forty who complained. The memo was reissued with a different word on the second line. Nothing else changed.
I wrote to my MP. The reply came in six weeks and was one paragraph long. But the writing felt like doing something.
We covered the gaps. We always do. Every officer on the wing took another post. The wing was quieter, and more brittle, and a lot more dangerous.
We found workarounds. The workarounds became the system. A year later, nobody could say how the wing had ever been staffed any other way.
I applied to three other services. I didn't get any of them. I stayed. The not-getting stayed too.
I applied for a transfer to an easier prison. I got it, and found that every prison is the same prison. I came back, eventually, to the one I knew.

title: The new one
text: A new recruit has been assigned to my wing. She's twenty-two. She's very good at the written tests and very scared of everything else. She calls me 'sir' and I can't make her stop.

outcomes.text: I taught her what I'd been taught. I stood next to her through the first fortnight. By the end of it she could read a landing. I've never been so proud of anything I haven't done myself.
I took her under my wing, and showed her the things nobody had shown me. She became a good officer. She wrote me a card on her tenth anniversary that said 'second rule is always the first'.

choices.label: Leave her to sink or swim

outcomes.text: She swam. I'd like to say it was because of me, but it was because she was good. I watched her from a distance for a year.
She sank. She resigned in the fourth month. I didn't speak to her about it, and have not stopped thinking about that.
I put her into a situation I knew would be difficult. She handled it well. When I told her she'd been set up, she looked at me for a long time. 'Thank you,' she said, and meant it.
I put her into the middle of a fight to see what she'd do. She froze. We never discussed it, but she asked for a different wing the next month.

title: Something's wrong with the count
text: The count is one short. It is 4.10 on a Friday and the roll call is wrong. I count again. There are 412 inmates in the building and 411 in front of me. Somewhere there is a man who isn't where he should be.

outcomes.text: I called it in. The siren went. Within eleven minutes the man was found in the laundry, in a cart, under a pile of sheets, with a very surprised expression. He'd been trying to get out through the van.
I raised the alarm. The count was repeated. He was found by the dogs two hours later, in the culvert beyond the second fence, wet and furious.
I checked the likely places. It took twenty minutes, and when I found him, he was asleep in the boiler house. Nobody ever knew. I've been very, very careful about the count ever since.
I checked quietly for half an hour. He was gone. By the time I raised the alarm he was a mile away. I was investigated and the finding was 'negligence'.
It was {co.first}'s count. I changed the number. Eleven minutes later he turned up in the library. We never discussed it. It's the nearest I've come to a debt of honour.
I fixed the count, and it caught up with us both in a week. A man in a grey suit asked me what I had been thinking. I said, 'About a friend.'

title: On watch
text: A man on my landing has been put on constant observation. He's sitting on the edge of the bunk with a blanket. He hasn't spoken in two days. It's three in the morning and I'm the only officer awake.

outcomes.text: I pulled up a chair to the door and talked about nothing: the football, the weather, a nickname I'd heard. At five he said, 'It's not the football.' We talked till the light came up. He is still alive.
I talked, and he talked back, a little. I wrote it all down. In the morning I gave the chaplain a note. It wasn't enough. But it was something, and it was all of me.

choices.label: Do the checks and nothing more

outcomes.text: I did the checks every fifteen minutes, as the order said. By dawn I'd done them all, and he was still there. It's what the book requires, and I tell myself it's enough.
I did the checks. At 6.10 the nurse arrived and took over. I never found out what happened to him. I wrote 'no concerns' on the sheet and I'd like not to think about it.
I called the duty nurse, who came in her slippers and sat down on the floor outside the door. She was there for three hours. She was better at it than I was.
I called, and the duty nurse took forty minutes. The man didn't wait. It was the first time I understood how thin the whole thing is.

title: What you bring home
text: Your partner says it quietly, at breakfast, over a cooling cup of tea. 'You've changed.' It's not an accusation. It's more like a doctor reading a chart.

outcomes.text: I told her about the man in cell nineteen. I told her about the sound. I had never said it aloud. She held my hand across the table, and we sat there until the tea was cold.
I told her some of it. Not all. She heard the rest in the pauses. It was the first night in a year I slept through.
I said I was fine. She said 'OK'. She said it in the way people say OK when it isn't. A year later she said it again, and I knew it was the last time.
I said it was only work. She nodded. It was a lie, and she knew, and we both agreed to live with it.
I booked two weeks. We went to the coast. For the first three days I woke at 5.40. On the fourth, I slept till nine.
I took a week. I came back with a tan and a sense of how long it had been since I'd noticed the weather.

title: It starts
text: It starts with a sound that doesn't belong: a tray, thrown. Then another, and a roar, and a banging along the whole length of the landing. The lights flicker. Somewhere below, a door gives. Every man in the building understands, at the same instant, that tonight is different.

outcomes.text: I ran with them. It's a thing that happens in the legs. The corridor was a river of men, and I was in it, and for the first time in years I was part of something larger than my own fear.
I went to the front and found a place at the edge of the front. The feeling was that of being a very small part of a very large decision.

choices.label: Lock myself in and stay down

outcomes.text: I pulled the mattress over me and put my back against the wall. The noise went on for hours. I counted the bangs. By dawn, I'd lost count, and the door had held.
I stayed in my cell and listened. A man I didn't know was crying for his mother. I couldn't help him. I've thought about it since.

I found three of them in the laundry, the youngest and the oldest and one who'd been in solitary. I got them up the back stairs to the chapel and bolted the door. We spent the night praying to a God none of us knew.
I went along the landing opening doors for the ones who couldn't. Some wouldn't leave. Some wouldn't stop thanking me. Nobody touched us.
A riot is a hole in the map. I went for the laundry stairs, with my head down, through the one door I knew would be open. It wasn't. I was at the wire before I knew what I'd done.
I used the chaos to get to the records office. I took a file. It was mine. I read it by torchlight, and what it said I will not repeat.

intel: My original file, read in the riot

title: The landing
text: The landing is a bonfire of mattresses, a storm of shouting, a dozen men with whatever they could find. Somewhere behind them are the officers, and a line of shields, and the sound of canisters. Someone hands you a pipe.

choices.label: Take it and hold the line

outcomes.text: I took it. I stood where I was told. A canister landed ten feet away, and I was coughing and blinded and holding a pipe, and an officer I had never seen came through the smoke with a baton. I do not remember much after that.
I took it and stood at the back. When the line broke, I ran. I got as far as the stairs.

choices.label: Put it down and slip away

outcomes.text: I put it down on the floor, politely, as though I'd been handed a cup of tea, and walked into a side corridor. Nobody stopped me. I was in my cell, with my back against the door, before the lights went out.
I put it down. A man next to me noticed, and said nothing. Later he came to my cell and said, 'You did right.' It was a strange benediction.

choices.label: Talk to the officers through the smoke

outcomes.text: I shouted. I said there were men who wanted to give up. An officer I knew by sight stopped, raised a hand, and the line paused. A dozen of us walked out of the smoke with our hands on our heads.
I tried to talk. Nobody heard. I was hit by a thrown bottle and dragged out by two men I had never met. I was grateful, and so were they.

title: The night in the cell
text: The cell door holds. The noise doesn't stop. At two in the morning a face appears at the hatch: a man from the next landing, bloodied, asking to be let in. He can't be. He's holding a blade.

outcomes.text: I let him in. He sat on the floor and shook. He'd done something that night he couldn't undo. We said nothing for three hours. In the morning I told the officers he'd been with me all night. It was a lie. He's still alive.
I let him in. He gave me the blade. I threw it out of the hatch. I never learned what he'd done with the other one.
I kept it shut. He banged on it for a long time. Then he stopped. I don't know what became of him. I've decided I don't want to know.
I shut the hatch. He shouted my name through it. It was the loneliest few minutes I've ever spent.
I shouted. An officer came, and the man ran, and the officer thanked me through the hatch, in a voice that was almost kind. I was a snitch from that moment, in the eyes of the landing.
I called out. The man was grabbed and dragged away, struggling. I watched through the gap. I felt both vindicated and sick.

title: The chapel
text: The chapel door is held shut with a pew. There are four of us on the floor, and one of them is bleeding from the scalp. Outside, someone is trying the handle, patiently, as a man tries the handle of his own front door.

outcomes.text: It was an old man with a bible and a bruise. He sat down among us. We shared a bar of chocolate, and a prayer none of us really meant, and it was as holy a night as any I've known.
It was a man with a pipe. He looked at the four of us on the floor, and the bleeding one, and lowered it. 'Not in here,' he said, and left. I will remember that sentence.
We held it. We held it for six hours. Whoever it was gave up. It was, I think, the hardest I've worked at anything, and I never saw what I was working against.
I held it with my back and my feet. At dawn there was a silence, and a gentle knock, and a voice that said, 'Officers.' I wept.
I prayed. I don't know to whom. It was the first prayer I'd said since childhood. It wasn't answered, but it didn't need to be.
I prayed with them. The bleeding one was a believer. He thanked me in the morning. I said I hadn't done anything. 'Yes you did,' he said.

title: The wire
text: The wire is a long way off in the dark, and above it the floodlights make a bright rectangle in the wet. A figure is running toward the fence from the other side of the yard. An officer in the tower has seen him.

outcomes.text: I ran. There's a point where a body knows more than the mind does. The light caught me when I was twenty feet from the fence. I stopped and lay down. They were very calm.
I ran, and I got to the fence, and I got a hand on it. I felt the old fear come up, and I let go. I'm not sure whether it was cowardice.
I walked back through the smoke with my head down and lay on the bunk. It was the right decision, and nobody can tell me otherwise.
I went back, and I regretted it for eleven years.
I shouted a direction. He turned. He was a boy, and he vanished into the dark. I never found out. I told nobody.
I went to him. He was already on the ground. An officer reached us at the same time. He was hurt but not badly. I stayed with him until the medics arrived.

title: The morning after
text: At dawn the building is quiet in a way I have never heard. The yard is full of smoke. A man in a suit is walking from cell to cell with a clipboard, asking each of us what we saw.

outcomes.text: I said it a hundred times that day, in the same words. A man in the next cell was removed in the afternoon, and I never saw him again. Nobody spoke to me for a fortnight.
I said I'd been in my cell. The investigator wrote it down and smiled, and I understood that he'd known the answer already.
I told him. I told him the names. I told him everything I'd seen, and it was an inventory of the worst night of my life. I was moved to a different wing that afternoon, with an escort.
I told him about the ones who'd been hurt. I didn't give a name that I didn't have to. It's a fine line, and I walked it, and I don't know where it led.
I said what the building had done to us. I said it in a measured voice. He wrote it all down, and I was told later that the report used my words. The warden was gone within the year.
I told him it was inevitable. He agreed, quietly. He said that was the problem.

title: The alarm
text: The alarm is a sound I've heard in drills a hundred times and never once like this. On the monitors, Block C is moving as one body. The wing sergeant's voice on the radio is thin. 'All available. All available. This is not a drill.'

outcomes.text: I ran. I was in the second rank at the stairwell with a shield and a baton and a radio shouting my number. The first rush hit and held, and it was an animal sound, and it was terrifying. I have never been so clear.
I went to the line. We held the stairwell. Behind me an officer was shouting commands in a voice I'd never heard her use. I held until the cry came to fall back.

choices.label: Fall back to the control room

outcomes.text: I locked the control-room door behind me, as I'd been trained. On the monitors I watched my colleagues fall back in order. Nobody blamed me. I blamed me.
I went to the control room. I did my job there, on the radio, directing the response. It was necessary. It did not feel like it was.

choices.label: Go back for the officer who is cut off

outcomes.text: {co.first} was on Block C when it went. I went in against the order, through the side stairs, with a master key. I found {co.him} in a cell with the door jammed. We came out together.
I went in for {co.first}. We got out, both of us, with scrapes. I was written up for leaving my post and commended for the same act on the same day.

title: Holding
text: The line has been holding for an hour. The inmates are throwing everything they have: trays, pipes, burning bedding. Behind us the response team is gearing up. The supervisor asks if you can hold another ten minutes.

outcomes.text: We held. It was seventeen minutes in the end. Someone near me went down, and someone else stepped in, and the rank closed. When the team came through, they were met by a silence and a wall of shields and a line of spent men.
I held, with the rest. It was the worst quarter of an hour of my life and also the most certain.
We pulled back a few steps and a gap opened. Three men came through it. They were stopped. It was close, and nobody was hurt, and the supervisor said nothing.
We withdrew in order. It was the right tactic, and it gave the inmates a yard of ground they didn't need to have.
I shouted over the noise, using a name. A man at the front stopped. He looked at me for a long moment, raised a hand and sat down in the middle of the stairwell. Eight others followed.
I tried. No one heard. A pipe hit my shield. The man who threw it later told me he was sorry.

title: The control room
text: The monitors show everything, in grey. On one, a group of inmates has taken three officers hostage on the second landing. On another, a fire is spreading in the laundry. The warden asks you what the priority should be.

outcomes.text: I sent the response team to the second landing. The fire spread. It was put out two hours later, with the loss of the laundry and a lot of paperwork. All three officers were recovered, bruised and alive.
I sent them for the hostages. We lost the laundry. We saved the officers. In the report, it said 'appropriate prioritisation', and I could not eat for two days.
I sent the fire team first. It was put out in twenty minutes. The hostages were released by the inmates, who, having made their point, were hungry. It could have gone the other way.
I sent them for the fire. When they reached the second landing, one of the officers had been badly hurt. I will think about that for a long time.
I split them. Half to the fire, half to the hostages. It was a gamble. Both worked. It's the closest I've ever come to being right by luck.
I split the team. Both missions failed to the degree they were underpowered. It was a lesson in a particular kind of arithmetic.

title: The cut-off wing
text: You and your colleague are in a stairwell on Block C with a cell door that won't open and a crowd of angry men coming up from below. {co.first} is bleeding from a gash above the eye. There is a window.

outcomes.text: It was a thirty-foot drop to the roof of the kitchen. We made it. {co.first} landed badly. We crawled along the roof to the next block and in through a skylight. It's the stupidest thing I've ever done and I'd do it again.
I got us out through the window, onto the roof. We sat there, in the dark and the smoke, till the response team arrived. {co.first} held my hand. Neither of us has ever mentioned it.
We stood in the stairwell, back to back, and held it for twenty minutes. Nobody got past. It was a victory of a kind. We both had to be stitched.
We fought. I'm not proud of it. I did what I had to. I saw faces I knew, and I saw them see me.
An inmate named {i.first} came up the stairs first, and he knew me. He stopped the others. 'Not these two,' he said. I will remember that for the rest of my career, and I will never know why.
I talked. It worked, partly. It bought us enough time for the team to arrive. The man who stood closest to me spat on the floor.

title: The inquiry
text: The riot lasted nineteen hours. The damage is estimated at four million. The review board has set up in the staff canteen with a flipchart and a very large pot of coffee. They would like your account.

outcomes.text: I told it plainly. I said what I'd seen and what I'd done. The panel wrote it all down. A line in the report says 'a clear and credible officer'. I'll take that.
I told them everything I'd seen. It included things I wasn't supposed to say. The report was a lot more critical than the one before it. The warden's replacement is grateful.
I said what everyone said. The board nodded. It was the sort of account that closes a file. A month later I was commended for my 'steady conduct'.
I said what the briefing said. It was true, and it wasn't the truth, and I knew the difference.
I told them it had been coming for years. I listed the vacancies, the locks, the staffing levels. It was all in a report I'd read in March. They looked at me with real alarm.
I said it was the cuts. They wrote that down, and the next year, a few of the cuts were reversed. It's the nearest I've come to changing something.

title: Cell fourteen
text: At 2.15 an inmate in cell fourteen has taken a nurse. He has a sharpened toothbrush against her neck. The wing is quiet in a way I haven't heard in years. The specialist team is forty minutes away. You are the nearest officer with training.

outcomes.text: I sat on the floor outside his door and used the voice. I said his name. I said I would listen. I listened for forty minutes.
I sat on the floor, and I asked him what he needed. He said he needed to speak to his daughter. The next forty minutes were the longest of my life.
I went in with two others. It was a bad idea executed well. The nurse was uninjured. The man was injured, badly, and it is in the report that the force was necessary. I do not look at the report.
I went in. The nurse was cut. She lived. She never spoke to me again, and I understood.
I held the corridor and waited. Forty minutes is a very long time. The nurse was brought out by the team. She was unharmed. I was the one who needed to sit down.
I waited. The team arrived late. The nurse had been cut by then. 'You did what the procedure said,' someone told me. It didn't help.

title: Talk him down
text: He says nothing for a minute, and then, in a flat voice, he starts to talk. What he says will tell you what he needs.

outcomes.text: It is a long conversation.

win.title: He put it down
win.text: He opened the door at 3.04 with the toothbrush in his open hand and his other hand over his face. The nurse walked out. He said, 'Is that it?' I said it was. We stood there in a pool of light, the two of us.

lose.title: It broke
lose.text: It went wrong at the end, over a word. He pressed. The nurse cried out. We went in. It was messy and fast and when it was over there was a cut and a ruined cell and a hush. She lived.

outcomes.text: I took it seriously. It went the way these things go.

win.title: He put it down
win.text: It took until dawn. When he opened the door, he asked for the chaplain. The nurse was unharmed. I was told afterwards that I'd saved a life. I thought only of the man.

lose.title: It broke
lose.text: He stopped listening at 3.40. The team arrived late. It was bad. The report says 'a tragic outcome', which is the sort of sentence you read for years.

outcomes.text: I said I could get his daughter on the phone. I wasn't sure I could. He said, 'Do it.' I got her.

win.title: A phone call
win.text: A child's voice came through the speaker in the corridor. It was all it took. He sat down, very slowly, and put the toothbrush on the floor. I've never known a quieter minute.

lose.title: She didn't answer
lose.text: The phone rang out. He heard it ring. I watched the thing go out of his face.

outcomes.text: I promised it. It was a risk. I got the call made.

win.title: A phone call
win.text: It was the right instinct. The call, the voice, the sitting-down. I filled in the paperwork, afterwards, with my hand shaking.

lose.title: Too late
lose.text: I couldn't reach her. He saw me with the phone, and read it on my face. It was over quickly after that.

choices.label: Stay silent and let him talk

outcomes.text: I said almost nothing. A man who hasn't been heard for a year will talk if you give him the silence. It took two hours. When he stopped, he put down the toothbrush.

win.title: Heard
win.text: He talked until his voice failed. Then he opened the door and sat down. It was the longest silence I ever kept, and the best.

lose.title: Not enough
lose.text: Silence isn't always a gift. He read mine as contempt, and acted. The rest is in a report.

outcomes.text: I listened. He cried, and then he shouted, and then he cried again. I held the line.

win.title: Heard
win.text: He put it down. I put out a hand and he took it. It was not in any procedure.

lose.title: Not enough
lose.text: It wasn't enough. I'll never know what would have been.

choices.label: Let the team handle it from here

outcomes.text: I stood down. The team arrived within a quarter of an hour. It was over in four minutes, and I stood in the corridor and watched my hands.
I handed it over. It was the right call. It didn't feel like a call I'd made.

title: In the yard
text: A man on the landing above has taken an officer. I can see him from the yard: a blade, an arm round a neck, a crowd gathering. The officer is a man I've never liked. His eyes find mine.

outcomes.text: I shouted up. I said the man's name. He looked down. I said, 'You don't want this.' Somehow it worked. The officer was released with a bruise, and I was beaten up by my own side that evening.
I walked up the stairs with my hands open. I talked to him for twenty minutes. He gave up the blade. It's the nearest I've come to being a hero, and it cost me everything I had on the landing.
I watched. Everyone watched. It ended without me, with a team and a lot of noise. The officer lived. I felt nothing, and then I felt it later.
I stayed where I was. It was over in an hour. The officer never forgot who watched.
I shouted nothing, but I was seen not to. Whatever happened, I'd be remembered on one side or the other.
I yelled with the crowd. It was an ugly thing to do. The officer was hurt, not badly. I got three days in the hole for it, and a name I'd rather not have.

title: The war
text: Two gangs have fallen out. It began with a card game and a remark, and by Thursday it's a policy. Every landing is divided. The mess hall is a map of who is allowed to sit where.

outcomes.text: I stayed in my cell, ate in my cell and spoke to no one. A war is a thing that happens to other people for as long as it can.
I kept to myself. Two men on my landing were hurt. Neither of them was me. I know how fragile that is.
I picked the side with the cleaner hands. It turned out they had none. But I belonged, and belonging in a war is warm.
I went in with my own gang. It's what we're for. Two weeks, four injuries, one death. The war ended with a handshake.
I talked to both sides. It took weeks, and a lot of tobacco. The war cooled. I was not thanked, but I was remembered by both.
I tried. They laughed, politely, and then someone sent a message that I should mind my own business. I did. I'd learned something.

title: A war on the wings
text: Two gangs have fallen out, and it is spreading. There have been three assaults in a week. On the staff side, the question is who to move, who to lock down and who to leave alone.

outcomes.text: I recommended a targeted lockdown. It worked, in the short term. The target wings were furious. For two months, every inmate on those landings looked at me as if I owed them.
I recommended it. The warden agreed. It cost us a month of good will, and it prevented, I think, a death.
I went to see the shot-callers on each side. I did it alone, without a radio. I said what I'd seen. I said that if it went on, we would all lose. They heard it. It went quiet for a year.
I talked to them, and made a few promises I could not keep. It bought us six months. I've never been entirely sure what I traded for it.
I looked the other way. Four men were hurt. One of them was a man I'd been trying to help. I wrote it up as 'inmate-on-inmate violence', which is a phrase that does a lot of work.
I did nothing, and the war burned itself out in three weeks. A man died. It is in the file as an incident, and it is in me as something else.

title: A new warden
text: A new warden has been appointed. At the first staff meeting, she says three things in a quiet voice: that things will change, that she does not intend to be liked, and that she has read every file in the building.

outcomes.text: I waited. Within six months, the changes were real: the lockdowns were shorter, the visits longer, a new rec yard planned. The building began, almost imperceptibly, to loosen.
I waited. Within six months it was clear that she was the real thing. A building can take years to know that.
I tested her. She was exactly as she'd said. It cost me a month of suspicion and gained me a strange sort of respect.
I tested her, and she saw it, and she wasn't offended. She asked for my opinion on the east landing. It was the first time a warden had.
I took the long view. A new warden is a new regime, and a new regime is a new chance. I adjusted my plans.

intel: A new regime: shorter lockdowns, longer visits

outcomes.text: I planned around her. If she was reformist, there'd be slack. If she was strict, there'd be gaps. Either way, I'd be ready.

title: A name and an instruction
text: The man I answer to hands me a name on a scrap of paper, folded small. 'Before the end of the month,' he says. 'You'll know how.' It is somebody I've eaten next to for a year.

outcomes.text: I did it in the stairwell at the change of shift. It took eleven seconds and it will take the rest of my life. I was promoted that week. I don't recommend it.
I did a version of it. I broke an arm and a rib, and I made sure he was not killed. The gang was satisfied. The man I'd hurt never spoke to me again.
I handed the paper back. 'I can't,' I said. He looked at me for a very long time. 'Then you can't be here,' he said. I was out within the week, and in danger for a year.
I told him no. It was a bad week. I took two beatings from men I'd called friends. But I kept the thing I would have lost otherwise.
I gave him a look and a sentence in the mess hall. He understood. Within a week he'd asked to be moved to protective custody. The gang wondered, and I wondered if they'd guessed.
I warned him, and it was not enough. He was hurt badly by somebody else. I was never sure whether I'd made it worse.

title: After the hole
text: I've been out of segregation for eleven days. I'm doing the things a person does: eating, walking, talking. They don't feel like mine. When an officer speaks to me, I take half a second to answer.

outcomes.text: I made myself do one thing a day, and no more. A walk. A page. A conversation about nothing. In six weeks I was almost a person.
I lay on my bunk and looked at the ceiling. It was a good ceiling. I learned to love the ceiling again, slowly.
A tired woman with a mug and a notebook. She listened, and nodded. 'It's very common,' she said. I'd never been so glad to be common.
She had a waiting list. I was seen in March. I told her about the hole. She wrote it down, and thanked me. It was something.
I joined the workshop and worked twelve hours a day for a month. I built a table. It was a very good table. I slept for the first time in a year.
I took up the gym and ran in place. My body hardened. My mind, slowly, caught up.

title: The form
text: The chaplain brings the news and the form. My mother died on Tuesday. The form is a request for 'compassionate temporary release', escorted, for the funeral. There's a box for my reasons, and it is three lines long.

outcomes.text: I filled it in in my best handwriting. The answer came back in four days: approved, with two officers and cuffs. I stood at the back of the church. My sister couldn't look at me. I didn't blame her.
I wrote what I felt, in three lines. It was denied: 'security considerations'. I stood at the cell window at eleven o'clock and watched the sky.
I couldn't bear the cuffs in the church. I stayed in my cell, and had my own service, in my head, and counted the hymns. A man on the landing slid a card under my door.
I didn't ask. I told myself it was for her sake. It was for mine.

choices.label: Write the eulogy to be read

outcomes.text: I wrote it over three nights. A cousin read it aloud. She told me afterwards that the church was silent. It was the best thing I've ever written, and I'd give it all not to have written it.
I wrote it, and the chaplain posted it. It was read out between the second hymn and the third. I'm told that people wept.

title: Before the board
text: The hearing is in nine days. There is a statement to write, a lawyer's letter to chase, an officer who may or may not give a reference. In the library, a man with experience tells you the thing nobody tells you: the board decides in the first four minutes.

outcomes.text: It took me a week. I wrote what I'd done and what I thought about it. I wrote that I didn't deserve to be forgiven, and that I hoped to deserve to be trusted. I read it out to a mirror.
I wrote what I felt, in plain words. My chaplain read it and cried. 'Say it exactly like that,' he said.

choices.label: Write what the board wants to hear

outcomes.text: I wrote it carefully, with a vocabulary I'd gathered from the other men's statements. It was a competent document. It had no heart at all, and the board will know.
I wrote what they wanted. It read like a leaflet. I have never felt so much like a fraud, and it's probably the most useful thing I'll ever write.

choices.label: Ask an officer for a reference

outcomes.text: {off.first} said yes, then no, then yes. The letter was two lines. It said I'd been 'no trouble'. It's a very good letter.
I asked {off.first}. He looked at me for a long time. 'I'd like to,' he said. 'I'll see what I can write.' It was a good letter.

title: Not this time
text: The envelope is thin. I know before I open it. 'Parole is denied.' There are three paragraphs of reasons and a date for the next review, and a sentence at the bottom that says I may appeal.

choices.label: Throw yourself into the next year

outcomes.text: I enrolled on two courses. I took the library job. I wrote to my daughter every week. I made myself a plan and followed it. By the next hearing, I'd become a different person, or so the file said.
I worked. I did every programme they'd put in front of me. When the next hearing came, the file was twice as thick.

It took me three weeks. I stopped eating and talking and answering the officers. A counsellor was called. I was put on observation. It was the lowest point of the sentence, and it ended, as these things do, without ceremony.
I wept. I punched a wall. I got a week in the hole for the wall. The wall did not seem to mind.
I thought about it for the first time as a real thing, in the dark, in a cell. I said it to nobody. But the idea sat there, and grew.

intel: The perimeter at night, as seen from the yard

outcomes.text: I stopped believing in the board. Not all at once, but with a quiet finality. I began to count the fence posts.

intel: The tower's rhythm at the change

title: A witness remembers
text: The call comes through the prison's legal-visits line. The investigator at the clinic sounds out of breath. 'One of the witnesses from your trial has been found. She wants to talk. She says she was pressured, and she's not sure of what she saw.'

outcomes.text: It cost every cent I had. The investigator travelled to three states. The witness signed a statement in front of a notary. It's on a form with a stamp on it. It's real.
I paid for the travel. It was the best money I've ever spent. The statement was short, and it had four sentences that I'd waited nine years to hear.
I waited. The clinic took four months to get to it. The witness had changed her mind again by then.
I waited. It was slow, but it was thorough, and when it came it was solid.
They let her come to the legal-visits room. We sat across a table. She looked at me for a long time. 'I'm sorry,' she said. 'I was twenty. I thought they knew.' I didn't say anything for a minute.
We met. She was nervous and kind. She apologised in a way that could have been a script and wasn't. The statement was signed by the end of the hour.

title: A hunger strike
text: The food has been getting worse for months, then worse again. On Monday, forty men on Block B refuse their trays. By Wednesday, it's two hundred. They are looking at the rest of us.

outcomes.text: I put my tray down untouched. By Friday I was dizzy. By Sunday I was lying on the bunk, in a quiet, bright place. The warden came on the seventh day with a list of concessions. It was a small victory, and I ate a slice of bread like a feast.
I joined. It's a stupid, wonderful thing to do. They fed us properly for three months afterwards, and then it slid.
I ate. It was bad, and I ate it, in front of them. I didn't think about it much at the time. I thought about it for years.
I ate my meal and said nothing. A man on the next table threw a roll at me. It was a gentle gesture, by the standards of the place.
I drew up the list of demands: food, medical, the roof. I got it to the warden through a chaplain. It was read, and it was acted on. Not enough, but acted on.
I wrote the demands in my best handwriting. I got three days in the hole as a ringleader. When I came out, the food was better.

title: The talent show
text: Once a year the chaplain organises a show in the chapel. It's the only night the wings mix. A man I don't know is about to sing, and someone is looking at me and saying, 'You should do something.'

outcomes.text: I did a poem I'd written, standing in the glare of a lamp. There was a silence, and then a sound I hadn't heard in years: the sound of two hundred men clapping because they wanted to.
I sang. I'm no singer. But I sang my mother's song, and the room joined in on the second verse, and for a minute it wasn't a prison.
I did the lights and the chairs and the tea. A man cried at the end, and I held the door for him. It was the best night of the year.
I helped set up. I saw things from behind the curtain that I'd never have seen from the floor: how scared people are before they perform.
I stayed in. The sound of the clapping came through the vents. I told myself it was nothing to do with me.
I stayed away. The next day, a man who'd been there told me what I'd missed. He was kind about it.

title: The first visit
text: She was two when I came in. She is eleven now, and she's sitting across a table from me with a bag of crisps and a face that is a mixture of my mother's and her mother's. 'Hi,' she says. 'Mum says you're my dad.'

outcomes.text: I told her what I did. I used the plainest words. She asked three questions, and the third was 'Are you sorry?'. I said yes. She nodded, and ate a crisp. We've written ever since.
I told her some of it. The rest I'll tell her when she's older. She said, 'OK,' and asked about my cell. It was the first normal conversation I'd had in years.

choices.label: Tell her it was a mistake

outcomes.text: I said it had all been a mistake. She looked at me for a long moment. She is very like her mother. 'That's what they all say,' she said. I've thought about that sentence for years.
