I told her. She was kind enough to believe me. I felt like a thief.
I asked about school. About her friends. About the dog. She talked for forty minutes, and I listened, and it was the best forty minutes of my life.
I asked her everything. She answered everything. At the end, she hugged me over the table, the guard looking away. I'll never forget the smell of her hair.

title: The papers
text: An envelope from a solicitor arrives with a window in it and my name typed on the front. It has a form and a pen and a note that says I need not attend. The date on the last page is three weeks ago.

outcomes.text: I signed. I did it in the visiting room, with a pen the officer lent me, and I gave the form back and said thank you. I went to the yard and walked round it four times.
I signed it that night. It took me two hours to find the right way to hold the pen. I slept on the floor.
I wrote a letter. I said what I felt, in four pages. She replied with one: 'I've waited as long as I can.' I signed the next day.
I contested it for a year. It wasn't about the marriage. It was about being asked.
She came. We sat there. We said nothing that mattered and everything that did. 'I'm sorry,' she said. 'So am I,' I said. And it was over.
She wouldn't. I understood. I signed the form and gave it back.

title: Five years
text: Today is the anniversary. Nobody mentions it. I mention it to nobody. I stand at the window with my forehead on the cool glass and try to remember the person who walked in.

outcomes.text: I made a list of what I'd done: what I'd learned, who I'd lost, who I'd met. It was longer than I expected. I put it in the Bible.
I counted the good things. There were four. I counted the bad. There were seventy. I put the paper away and began again the next morning.
I wrote a letter to myself in five years' time, and gave it to the chaplain. He promised to keep it. He has.
I made a mark on the wall, by the bed, with a pin. There are other marks. I'm not the first.
I did the day as usual. I ate and worked and slept. In the evening a man I barely knew put a biscuit on my bunk and left without a word.
I did the day as usual. It's the best way, I think.

title: The last year
text: There are twelve months left. It's strange how heavy they are. A man in the next cell has stopped sleeping. Another has started to cry at nothing. The closer the gate, the louder the walls.

outcomes.text: I started a list: a room, a job, a bank account. I wrote to a hostel. I asked the chaplain to find me a name. By the last month I had something I'd almost call a plan.
I did the programmes the staff recommended: the resettlement course, the job club. A woman from a charity said she'd meet me at the gate. I didn't believe her until she did.
I did something stupid. I broke a rule I'd never broken before, for no reason at all, and was put on report. It isn't uncommon. It's the building saying goodbye.
I did nothing at all for six months. I lay on the bunk. A friend took me by the hand and walked me round the yard, and said, 'You're going to be fine.' He was wrong. But he was kind.
I spent the last weeks saying goodbye to every person I had met. It was an exhausting, joyful, ridiculous kind of tour.
I gave away my things: the radio, the books, the plastic mug. I kept the picture. On the last night I wrote down every name I could remember.

title: Cold feet
text: One of the crew is not sleeping. In the exercise yard {c.first} keeps looking at the fence and then at his feet. When he sees me, he starts, as if I'd come up behind him.

outcomes.text: I took him aside and told him the whole thing, again, step by step. By the end he was nodding. I couldn't tell if I'd calmed him or if I'd made it worse.
I told him what it would be like on the other side. His eyes filled. 'I want to see my kids,' he said. 'So do I,' I said.
I told him he was out. He took it badly. For a week he stared at me across the mess hall, and I watched my own back.
I told him he was out, and I told the others why. It was necessary, and I felt like a bastard, and a week later there was a message under my door that said 'thanks'.
I made it clear to him what would happen if he did. I did it with a calm voice and an open face, and he understood. I didn't like what I'd become.
I had a friend of mine speak to him. He was very persuasive. The man did not speak to anyone for a month.

title: More than we agreed
text: The man on the inside has asked for more. It's a message in a library book: the original price plus half again, and a favour I don't understand. 'Things have got harder,' he says. They always have.

outcomes.text: I paid. I sold everything I could sell and borrowed the rest. He took it with a calm face. I did not feel the plan was safer, only dearer.
I paid. The price of a thing like this has no ceiling. It's the one law I'm sure of.
I told him no. For a week I heard nothing at all. Then a note said 'OK', and nothing more. I don't know if it's good news.
I said no. He said he'd think about it. The silence that followed felt like a decision.

choices.label: Tell him I know about him

outcomes.text: I let him know that I knew what he was. He went pale. 'There's no need for that,' he said. It worked. It also taught him exactly how I'd behave if it went wrong.
I let him know what I could say. It was a threat, and a bad one. He paid it back in kind, within the week.

title: People are talking
text: A man I barely know stops me on the stairs. 'I hear you've got something planned,' he says, pleasantly, as though he were asking about the football. He looks at the wall behind me and says, 'Just so you know.'

outcomes.text: I said it was nonsense. I said it in a flat voice. He nodded, and smiled, and walked on. A day later the whole of my landing was in a particular kind of silence.
I laughed. It was a poor laugh. He laughed too. We both knew.
I brought him in. He was clever, and useful, and a liability. But a man who knows is safest when he's inside.
I told him I'd think about it. A week later I added him to the crew, with some misgivings. They were justified.
I paid him in tobacco. He took it. He didn't say another word about the plan, but he looked at me differently ever after.
I did what had to be done. I'm not going to describe it. I'd call it a cost.

title: A knock on the door
text: A knock on the door at nine in the evening. Two knocks, a pause, a third. It isn't the landlady's. I stand with my back to the wall and my hand on the back of a chair, and I don't breathe.

outcomes.text: I stood there for a quarter of an hour. The knock came again, once, and then footsteps going away. In the morning there was a leaflet for a pizza place on the mat.
I waited. They went away. I never found out who they were. I moved the next day.
A woman from the flat below, with a parcel that had been left with her. She smiled and said 'Hello, neighbour' and went away. I had to sit down.
A young man with a clipboard, from the council, wanting to ask if I was on the electoral roll. I said I wasn't. He wrote it down. I moved the next day.
I was over the wall and into the lane before the second knock. I walked until it got light. It was a false alarm. I moved on anyway.
I went out the back and into the arms of a cat, a dustbin and a lot of mud. It wasn't dignified. It was safe.

title: Someone looked twice
text: In a corner shop a woman looks at me, then at the rack of newspapers, and then at me again. She doesn't say anything. She is holding a loaf of bread, and she hasn't moved.

outcomes.text: I put down my basket and walked out. I walked for an hour in a loop, and then another hour in a different loop, and got home by a route no one could follow. I do not know whether she called.
I left without hurry. In the mirror of a parked car I saw her at the window. She was on the phone.
I said, 'I know what you're thinking.' She said, 'I think you're a man who looks like someone I saw on the news.' I said 'People tell me that.' She smiled, and bought her bread, and I walked out.
I told her something close to the truth. She listened. She said, 'I won't say anything,' and she didn't. I'll never know why.
I was on a bus by midnight. I changed again at dawn. By the time anyone looked, I was in another county.
I left that night, with a rucksack and no plan. It was the wrong thing and I knew it, and the right thing too.

title: A voice from before
text: The phone in the hall rings and rings. On the eleventh I pick it up and say nothing. 'It's me,' says a voice I have known for twenty years. 'I know where you are. I'm not going to say.'

outcomes.text: We talked for an hour. They told me about everyone. They told me the investigators had been, twice. They said they hadn't said a word. I believed them, and that was the only thing in the world I did.
They told me to run. They told me the name of a person in another city. I wrote it on my hand.
I hung up. They called back four times. I did not answer. I moved the next day.
I hung up, and cried for an hour. I could not afford to be found, even by someone who loved me.
They sent what they had, in an envelope with no return address. It was a lot. It was too much. I knew I'd regret it.
They sent a few hundred. It came to a poste restante. I checked it three times before I collected it.

title: A tip
text: An inmate stops me at the end of the landing and speaks without moving his lips. 'Boss. Friday. The laundry. That's all I'll say.' He is already walking away.

outcomes.text: I searched the laundry that night with two officers. We found a stash: tools, a phone, a very long length of cord. It was the second-best catch of my year. The inmate who gave me the tip got a better cell.
I acted on it. We found something, though it wasn't what I expected. It was a lot of cigarettes and a note that said 'Nice try'. He had been playing a game.
I waited and watched. On Friday I saw exactly what he'd meant. A parcel changed hands in the laundry. I let it go, to see where it went. It went to a man I hadn't suspected.

intel: A handover route through the laundry

outcomes.text: I waited. Nothing happened on Friday. On Saturday, a man was found with a broken arm in the laundry. I was told, afterwards, that I should have acted.
I ignored it. On Friday, in the laundry, a man was stabbed. It's in the file as an unforeseeable incident. I've never been able to accept that.
I ignored it. Nothing happened. I'll never know whether that's luck, or whether he was lying.

title: The man who is going home
text: {i.first} has been on my wing for nine years. He is leaving on Friday. He asks if I'd shake his hand. It's against a number of rules.

outcomes.text: I shook it. His hand was dry and small and warm. 'Look after the young ones,' he said. I said I'd try. I've never forgotten the way he said it.
I shook it, in the corridor, behind the door, where no camera could see. He cried, and so did I, and we both pretended not to.
I said, 'Good luck.' He nodded. I watched him go through the gate, small and grey, with a plastic bag. I felt like a clerk.
I kept to the rules. He understood. He walked out with his head up. It was a good dignity, and I took none of it.
I wrote it on the back of a bus ticket. It was the worst possible idea. He called me from a payphone six years later, and said, 'I wanted to say thanks.' He'd opened a garage.
I gave him a number. I regretted it every day for a month. Then I forgot. Then he called, a year later, from a pub, drunk and happy.

title: Over the wall
text: A small black drone is crossing the yard at dusk, trailing something. The tower shouts. It drops a package behind the workshop and rises over the wire. There's a man at the window of Block D with his hand over his mouth.

outcomes.text: We found it in four minutes. Phones, drugs, a razor. The investigation took six months and led nowhere. The drone is in a glass cabinet in the staff room now.
I got there first. There were three phones, a bag of white powder and an envelope with my name on it. I will not say who it was from.
I let the package lie. Someone else would pick it up. I had a wife and mortgage and I didn't want the paperwork. A week later, a man on Block D had a phone.
I looked away. It's a decision I make about twice a year. It's never the right one and it's never the wrong one.
I took a phone. It was the most expensive thing I ever bought. I was never discovered, but I walked the landing for a year afraid of the sound of my own keys.
I took a share. I took it quietly and I told no one. I've never forgiven myself, and I've never been found out.

title: Walk out
text: The union has called a walk-out. The government has called it illegal. On the wing, the inmates have heard, and the building has the particular hush of a place that's wondering what you'll do.

outcomes.text: I walked out with forty others. We stood at the gate in the rain with banners. The press came. The government blinked, eventually, and we got six more officers. I got a letter on my file and a story to tell.
I walked out. It lasted three days. We got a promise and a pay rise of two per cent. Two officers lost their jobs. I've never been sure if it was worth it.
I crossed the picket. A colleague spat at my feet. I was thanked by the governor and avoided by the staff room for three years.
I went in. I told myself it was for the inmates. It was partly true. It was also partly for the pension.
I stayed at home. It was a quiet, cowardly sort of solidarity. Nobody blamed me, and nobody thanked me.
I called in sick, and spent three days in the garden. For the first time in eight years I heard the birds.

title: Served
text: A process server finds me in the car park and hands me a thick envelope. An inmate has sued me, personally, in federal court. He says I denied him medical treatment on a night in October. I remember that night. I remember it very well.

outcomes.text: I hired a lawyer. The case took two years. In the end, the judge found for me on every count. I felt neither relief nor vindication. I'd have paid the man to say sorry.
I fought it. The union paid. We won. The inmate was sent a letter, and wrote back, and I read it at my kitchen table for an hour.
It was settled for a sum I would have found unspeakable a year before. The lawyer said it was the clever thing. I felt that it was a confession.
I settled. The sum was a year's salary. It bought silence, and I paid the price of knowing what it was for.
I took the stand. I said what had happened, including the part that wasn't in the report. The jury was out for forty minutes. They found against me. I was not surprised, and I was oddly relieved.
I told the truth. It cost me the case and a year of my life. Afterwards, the inmate came up and shook my hand in the corridor of the court. I've never understood why.

title: What do you do at work
text: My daughter's school has a 'what our parents do' week. She's asked me three times what to say. I've said 'public service'. She says that's not an answer. Tonight she says: 'Do you hurt people, Dad?'

outcomes.text: I sat on the edge of her bed and told her. I told her that the people I look after have done bad things, that some of them are very sad, and that my job is to keep everyone safe. She asked if I was scared. I said sometimes.
I told her. She listened with great seriousness. 'I'll tell them you keep people safe,' she said. I was far too moved to answer.
I changed the subject. She noticed. She always does. She told her class I worked in an office, and the teacher, who knew, said nothing.
I told her it was boring, grown-up stuff. She sighed, and drew a picture of me in a cap. It looked like an airline pilot.
I let her hold them, in the kitchen. She weighed them in both hands. 'They're heavy,' she said. 'Yes,' I said. It's the best thing I've ever said about the job.
I showed her the keys, and she hung them on the doorknob and said they were the best keys in the world. I've never forgotten.

title: The dinner
text: They hold the retirement dinner on a Thursday in a function room above a pub. There is a cake in the shape of a set of keys. The speech is shorter than it should be, and several people say my name wrong. I find that I'm not sure what I feel.

outcomes.text: I stood, and said thirty years in a sentence, and everyone laughed at the right place. Then I said something true, and the room went quiet. I thanked the ones who weren't there to hear it.
I made a short speech. I thanked the night staff. I thanked the inmates, which no one had expected. The room clapped for a long time.
I left after the cake. In the car park I sat in my car and did nothing for twenty minutes. I wasn't sad, exactly. I was waiting for something to stop.
I went home before the speeches. My wife said nothing and made a cup of tea.

choices.label: Sit with the ones who stayed

outcomes.text: I sat with five officers, from the years before, and we talked about the dead and the dying and the ones who got away. It was the best evening I've had in twenty years.
I sat with the old team. We told each other the stories. They got bigger and funnier. By midnight we were laughing about things that had made us weep.

title: The cat in the yard
text: A thin tabby has been getting through the wire for a month. It sleeps in the workshop. This morning there are four men around it, and nobody has said a word, and nobody has tried to move it.

outcomes.text: I saved a corner of my bread. The cat accepted it. For two years it was the nearest thing the wing had to a mascot. Men who didn't speak to each other spoke about the cat.
I fed it. Another man gave it a name. A third built it a bed from a box. It's the one thing in the building that no officer ever mentioned.

It let me. It was warm. It smelled of oil and dust. I held it for a minute, and the four men watched, and none of us said anything. I had forgotten what it was to hold a living thing that wasn't afraid.
I picked it up. It bit me. I laughed, and so did the others. It was the first time I'd laughed in a month.
I told an officer. The cat was removed that afternoon, and I never found out where it went. I was not popular.
I reported it. The officer looked at me for a long time and said, 'You're a strange one.' The cat stayed.

title: The heat
text: The thermometer in the officers' station reads thirty-nine. In the cells it is higher. The windows don't open. Men lie on concrete in their shorts and do not move. The tension is something you can feel on your skin.

outcomes.text: I lay on the floor with a wet towel and my eyes closed, for eleven days. It ended, as it does. I learned that I could do eleven days of anything.
I endured. A man two cells down was taken to the infirmary on the sixth day. I heard the trolley. I put the towel over my face.
I got the kitchen to leave out the ice. I got an officer to turn a blind eye to buckets. We kept the landing alive. I'd earned something, though I didn't know what.
I did the rounds with a bucket. The ones who'd been rude to me drank first. It's an odd sort of leadership.
A heatwave is a distraction. In the long afternoon, with everyone half asleep, I walked the whole of the east side of the wing and noted what I saw.

intel: The east stairwell camera is unplugged in the heat

outcomes.text: Half the cameras were out of order, the other half were pointed at the wall. I counted them. It was an education.

intel: Half the cameras fail in a heatwave

title: The list
text: A list goes up on the noticeboard at six. My name is on it. 'Transfer: 0700 Thursday.' Nobody says where. Nobody ever does. I have three days to say goodbye to a building I have hated for years and can't picture leaving.

outcomes.text: The bus left at seven. I watched the old building go past through a gap in the blind. It was smaller from outside. The new place was brighter, noisier, newer, and had no history with me at all.
I accepted it. The new place was worse, which I had expected, and in some ways better, which I hadn't. For the first time in years nobody knew who I was.
I wrote to the governor. I wrote to my lawyer. The list was revised. A different man was moved in my place, and I never felt right about it.
I fought it. It was a long week and a futile one. I went anyway.

choices.label: Make the most of the last days

outcomes.text: I said goodbye to everyone. I gave away my books and my radio and a half-written letter. I walked the wing at midnight with my hands behind my back, like a visitor.
I spent the days walking the yard. I had a last conversation with a man I'd hardly spoken to in six years. He said, 'I'll miss you.' I was surprised to find I would miss him.

title: The tournament
text: The chaplain has organised a football tournament, the first in four years. There are eight teams, one from each landing. The warden has decreed that the winner will have an extra hour of rec every day for a month.

outcomes.text: I was a midfielder on a bad team. We lost 6-0 in the first round and had the best time I've had in years. I was kicked in the shin by a murderer. We shook hands afterwards.
I played in goal. We reached the final and lost on penalties. I saved two. The other landing carried me round the pitch on their shoulders for a minute anyway.
It's a thankless job. I gave eleven yellow cards and one red. The red was to a man who'd done something I'll not describe. Nobody argued.
I refereed. Four hundred men watched me make decisions. For two hours, I was the most important man in the building. It's a heady feeling.
A man on the second landing ran the book. I put down three packs on the underdogs. They won. I was owed an enormous amount of tobacco and a very mild threat.
I bet, and lost. The sum was small, and it was, as such sums are, enormous.

title: Getting old in here
text: The doctor says the word 'geriatric' in a clinical voice. It's the first time I've heard it used about me. Men my age are going into the infirmary and not coming back. The stairs have become a negotiation.

outcomes.text: I walked the yard every morning until I couldn't. The doctor said it was good for me. A young man fell in beside me. We never talked about it, but we both knew why.
I took up the gym again. The young ones watched, in the way you watch a very old dog trying to run. By the end of the year I was ahead of them on the bench.
I moved to the lower bunk. I took up the library's large-print section. I made my peace with the infirmary. It was a good peace.
I accepted it. I sat in the sun, on the bench by the wall, and watched the young men run. It was a kind of retirement.
I thought of the world outside, and what I'd do in it, if I ever saw it. The answer was nothing much. Walk. Sit. Ride a bus. It was a surprise to realise it was enough.
I wrote to a care home that takes ex-offenders. They said, 'We'll see.' It was the first 'we'll see' that hadn't felt like a no.

title: An order I don't like
text: {sup.first} brings word from the warden's office. All officers are to stop doing something that has kept the wing quiet for six years. It's an ordinary memo, with a signature at the bottom. Everybody who reads it knows it will cause trouble.

outcomes.text: I followed it. The wing went wrong in a month. When it did, nobody remembered the memo. I remembered it.
I followed it, and said nothing. In October it all went off. The warden said, afterwards, that the memo had been 'misapplied'.
I carried on as before. The wing stayed quiet. I was never caught. It's a sort of professional integrity, I think, to know which orders to break.
I carried on. A colleague reported it. The finding was 'a failure to comply', and a note went on my file.
I wrote a one-page memo of my own, with numbers. The warden read it. He called me in. 'You're right,' he said. 'And you've made enemies.' The order was changed. I had.
I challenged it. The reply came back in a week, three lines long. It was to the effect that I could keep my views to myself.

title: A phone on the landing
text: A phone rings in the walls. It is a small, familiar sound. It has been ringing, every night, for a week. Tonight I follow the ring to cell twenty-two and find a boy of nineteen with the phone at his ear and the face of someone caught in a church.

outcomes.text: I took it. I took the SIM, the battery, the lot. I wrote a clean report. He said 'Please, boss, it's my mum.' I didn't know what to say. I gave him a form for the official phone.
I took it. He cried. I took it anyway. It's the right thing to do and it never feels it.
I turned and faced the wall for two minutes. When I turned back, he'd hung up. I put the phone in my pocket. 'Thank you,' he said. We didn't mention it again.
I let him finish. The conversation was short. I could hear a woman's voice, high and thin. When he hung up, I took it. 'Thank you,' he said, three times.
He told me. It was a name I knew. It led to a ring, and a search, and a man in an office. It was a good bust. It was also the end of a rare quiet period.

intel: A phone route through the kitchen

outcomes.text: He told me nothing. I took the phone. A week later someone else's name was in the book.

title: A night like any other
text: At 2.40 an inmate in cell nine says he is in pain. He says it in the voice of a man who says it every night. The nurse is asleep in the infirmary, and the doctor is off site. I have to decide whether this is a night like any other.

outcomes.text: She came in her slippers, took one look at him, and called an ambulance. It was a ruptured appendix. He lived. She said, 'You did the right thing', and went back to bed. I couldn't sleep.
I called her. She said it was nothing, and then, on looking, that it was something. The ambulance took forty minutes. He lived. He sent me a card.
I came back in an hour. He was worse. The ambulance took forty minutes, and he did not have forty minutes. An inquest followed.
I came back in an hour. He was asleep. It was nothing. It's my fate, I think, to be right about the wrong things.
I stayed with him for two hours. I talked about nothing. By morning he was better. It was nothing. It's the kind of nothing you do for years.
I sat with him. He told me about his mother. By dawn, he was asleep, and I was a different person. I don't know which of us got more out of it.

title: What the gang remembers
text: The gang does not forget. It has been a year since the thing, and the man who runs the landing is waiting for me by the stairs with that mild expression that means he's decided.

outcomes.text: A favour, as promised. I did it without comment. He watched me do it and said nothing at all. It was the nearest thing to a blessing.
I paid it, and it cost more than I'd expected. But he nodded, and the account was closed, and I was one of them in a way I had not been before.
I asked for protection for a friend. It was granted, for a price. I'd never known a transaction like it.
I asked for a transfer to a quieter landing. He considered it. It was granted. The look he gave me afterwards was almost respectful.
I walked away. He let me. I was hit twice, quickly, in the stairwell, by men who looked embarrassed. It was settled, in the way these things are.
I walked. I walked into three months of avoiding stairwells. In the end, nobody could be bothered.

title: The man you owed
text: He's out now. I heard on the grapevine that he was waiting at the gate for someone else. The man I once owed is sitting on a bench in the visiting room, with his hat on his knee, wanting a word.

outcomes.text: I told him I'd been wrong. I told him I was sorry, and that if I'd had it, I'd have paid. He nodded for a long time. 'That's all right,' he said. 'I'd have done the same.' We were square.
I told him. He said he'd forgotten. I'm not sure I believed him. We shook hands.
I avoided him until he left. A year later I heard that he'd died. I should have talked.
I avoided him. It worked for three weeks. In the fourth, he found me in the library. We didn't speak, and it was worse.
I'd saved it for years. I counted it into his hand. He stared at it. 'You didn't have to,' he said. I said I did.
I paid every cent, with interest. It cost me everything I had. I slept well.

title: A letter from the kid
text: A letter arrives with a stamp I don't recognise. It's from the boy I looked out for. He has a job, a flat and a small fierce handwriting. 'I thought you'd like to know,' he says.

outcomes.text: I wrote four pages. I said how proud I was. I said what I'd learned from him. A reply came in a fortnight, and a photograph. It's on the wall above my bunk.
I wrote back the same evening. I didn't know I had that many words in me. We have been in touch ever since.
I put the letter under my pillow and read it every night for a month. I told no one. It was the best news I had.
I kept it private. A man could do worse than have something nobody else knows about.
I asked him to find my daughter. He did. It took him a year, and he sent me her address and a note: 'She's well.' I couldn't breathe.
I asked him to send me books. A box arrived within the month. It had a dictionary, a novel and a pack of biscuits.

title: The officer retires
text: {off.first} is retiring. There's a cake in the staff room and a card on the noticeboard that the inmates are not supposed to sign. A line has formed, quietly, behind the officer's station.

outcomes.text: I signed my name. It was a small gesture. He read it, silently, and nodded. 'Take care of yourself,' he said. I've not forgotten.
I signed it. The man behind me wrote a long message. I read it upside down and couldn't stop smiling.
I said nothing. He left on a Friday. A new man took his place on Monday. I missed him for a long time.
I stood at the back and watched. He didn't look at me. Perhaps that was kindness.

choices.label: Ask him for one last thing

outcomes.text: I asked him for a character reference for the board. He said yes, at once. It was the best letter in my file.
I asked if he'd say a word for me. He said, 'I already have.' I didn't know what he meant. A year later, I did.

title: A graduation
text: A photograph comes in an envelope. A young person in a gown and a flat hat, squinting into the sun on a lawn. On the back, in pencil, a single line: 'Thought you should see.'

outcomes.text: I had it framed by the workshop man, out of balsa wood. It's the best thing I own. It hangs where the light falls on it at four in the afternoon.
I put it up on the wall. I look at it every day. I've never been prouder, and I've never felt so absent.
I wrote the best letter of my life. A reply came back, shorter. It said, 'Thanks, Dad.' I read it a hundred times.
I wrote it, but I could not think of an ending. I sent it without one. They wrote back and said it was fine.
I looked at it for a long time, and then put it face-down. It was too much. I took it out again that night.
I put it away. I couldn't have it near me. I couldn't have it far.

title: The hearing
text: The hearing is set for the fourteenth. It will be in a small, wood-panelled court, with a judge, two lawyers and a clerk. My lawyer calls it 'the best chance you will ever have'. I do not sleep.

outcomes.text: We met four times. We went through every question the prosecutor might ask. On the day, I answered each one in a steady voice. The judge listened for a long time. The ruling was reserved.
We prepared for six weeks. On the day, the prosecutor made a mistake with a date. My lawyer pounced. It was over in an hour. The judge said, 'I think we've heard enough.'
We prepared hard. On the day, the court rejected the new evidence as inadmissible. It was a disaster, and I went back to my cell and lay down for a week.
I stood up and spoke, without notes. I spoke for eleven minutes. The room was silent. When I sat down, the judge took off her glasses and cleaned them. The ruling came six weeks later.
I spoke. It was too long, and too angry, and too true. The judge was patient. The prosecutor smiled. It didn't go my way.
I asked to be excused. The clerk wrote it down. The lawyer represented me. The hearing took an hour, and I spent it in my cell with a book I did not read.
I stayed away. My lawyer said later it was just as well. The ruling was reserved, with a note that the court would consider further submissions.

title: The deal's long shadow
text: It has been a year since the man in the good coat came. The landing has changed. People stop talking when I come in, and the ones who don't are the ones who've decided.

outcomes.text: I kept my head down and my back to a wall. A year of that and the air cleared. It never cleared completely.
I did exactly what I'd always done. They saw it, eventually, and they decided it was dull. It's the greatest compliment the place can pay.
I found one, an old man in the library who didn't care. We played chess, and he lost every game and told me who to look out for. I've never been more grateful for a man's indifference.
I made a friend in the infirmary. A man with no future and a very good memory. He told me everything I needed to know.

intel: Who is angriest about the deal

outcomes.text: I found the man I'd named. I told him I was sorry. He looked at me for a very long time. Then he spat. Then he sat down, and talked. It was the strangest conversation of my life.
I wrote to him. He didn't reply. But three years later, a message came through a chaplain: 'Tell him it's all right.' I wept.

title: The sister calls back
text: The phone rings on my night off. A woman's voice, unsteady. She introduces herself as the sister of a man on Block B. She says, 'Thank you for what you did.' Then she says, 'There's something else I need to ask.'

outcomes.text: She wanted a letter taken in. A small thing. It was a letter and it said 'we love you'. I took it in. I am more at ease with this than I should be, and I am less at ease than I look.
She wanted me to take a message to her brother. I did. It was kind, and it was wrong, and I did it again the following month.
I said no. I said I was sorry. She said, 'I understand.' She hung up. I thought about her all night.
I said no. I told her I'd done too much already. She thanked me and wished me well. It was the end of a small story, and I didn't like how it felt.
I wrote it up in the morning. The sergeant read it and nodded. 'Good,' he said. The brother was moved. I'm not sure I did the right thing. I'm sure I did the correct thing.
I reported it. The sister was cautioned. The brother was transferred. I never learned how they got on.

title: The footage
text: The footage turns up in a review. It's a landing camera, grainy, from March. You are in the frame for eleven seconds. A man in a suit has it paused on the moment where your arm is raised.

outcomes.text: I explained every second of it. He listened. At the end he said, 'Thank you. I can see that.' It was cleared, in the end, with an advisory note. I kept my job and lost my sleep.
I told him what I'd seen, and what I'd felt, and where I'd gone too far. He wrote it down. The union rep winced. The outcome was a warning.
I denied it. I said the footage didn't show what it showed. He played it again. It showed exactly what it showed. I was suspended without pay for a fortnight.
I denied it, and the denial became a second charge. The case was closed in my favour, on a technicality, and I have never felt so dirty.
I resigned. I couldn't face the process. I was gone within the month. I've never gone back, though I've walked past the gates.
I handed in my keys. A younger man took my place. I got a letter that said 'we regret'.

title: A letter from outside
text: A letter arrives at my home address. No return address. It's from the man who was on my wing and who has now been released. It says only, 'I got out. I wanted you to know that I'm doing well. I'm sorry for what I put you through.'

outcomes.text: I burned it in the sink. It was the right thing to do, and it was the saddest thing I did that year.
I burned it. I did not tell my partner. The ashes went down the plughole, and I stood there for a long time.
I kept it in a drawer. I read it twice a year, on the anniversary and on the day of his birthday. It's the only secret I have.
I kept it. It was the proof that something good had come out of the building. I couldn't throw it away.
I replied with three lines. We exchanged four letters in all. It ended, the way these things do. I'm glad I did it, and I'm glad it ended.
I wrote back. It was an odd correspondence, between an ex-officer and an ex-inmate. We understood each other better than I'd imagined.

title: Her promotion
text: A note on the noticeboard: the recruit I trained eight years ago has been made up to sergeant. She comes to find me in the car park, a bit self-conscious, with a bottle in a paper bag. 'I wanted to say thanks,' she says.

outcomes.text: We drank it in the car, in the dark, from paper cups. We talked for an hour about nothing and everything. It's one of the three best nights I've had in the job.
I accepted it, and told her to keep her eyes open. 'Second rule's always the first,' she said. I had no idea she'd remembered.
I told her to keep it for a day she'd need it. She laughed and nodded. I think she has.
I said, 'Keep it. You'll want it more than I do.' She looked at me, and then at the bottle. 'You're right,' she said.
I told her the thing I wish I'd been told: that it gets easier, and that is the problem. She was quiet for a while. 'I know,' she said.
I told her about the cost. I told her what it takes out of you. She listened with her whole face.

title: The letter from the family
text: A letter arrives at the staff office, forwarded unopened. It's from the family of the man in cell nineteen. It's two pages. It's handwritten. It begins, 'Dear Officer, we wanted to thank you.'

outcomes.text: I read it three times. I've kept it in the lining of my wallet for years. It's the best thing anyone's written to me.
I read it. I read it to my wife. She cried. I did not, which is itself a kind of fact about me.
I wrote a letter that took me a week. I said what I could. A reply came, shorter. It said, 'Thank you for writing.' I've never been as relieved.
I wrote back. It was a short note. I didn't know what to say. I said what I thought, which was that I was sorry.
I couldn't face it. I put it in a drawer. In a year I would read it. In ten I would cry.
I put it away. There are things you can't carry on a shift.

title: The tip pays off
text: The man who gave me the tip last year has found me on the landing again. He doesn't look happy. 'You owe me,' he says quietly, as though noting the weather.

outcomes.text: I did him a small favour: a call to his mother. It didn't seem like much. In his world it was a diamond.
I got him a transfer to a quieter wing. He thanked me with a nod. I felt the new weight on my back, the weight of a debt that wouldn't be repaid.
I put him on the list for protective custody. It took a form and a signature. It saved his life, I think. I'll never know.
I kept an eye on him for a year. He had a hard time. He never asked for anything again.
I told him I owed him nothing. It was true. It was also cruel. He nodded. He never spoke to me again.
I told him I'd done my job and he'd done his. He left. A week later he was found with a broken jaw. I'll never know whether that was my fault.

title: Fresh fish
text: A year. It's a small, hard number. You've learned the count, the queue, the rules about where to put your eyes. You've seen what a man can be broken by and what he can bear. In the yard one evening, an old hand nods at you in a way that means something has changed.

outcomes.text: I nodded. It was the smallest thing. But a landing is made of such things, and from that night on, a few people did not look through me.
I nodded back. It was a signal and I'd answered it. I've learned a language I can't write down.
I kept walking. It's a decision, to stay unseen. For another year I was an empty uniform. It's safe. It's very lonely.
I walked on. I was learning that the best way to survive is to leave no mark. It was working.
He laughed. 'It means you're still here,' he said. It was the first thing anyone had told me that day that I believed.
He looked at me for a while. 'It means keep going,' he said. And I did.

title: Whose side?
text: Nobody gets through this place alone. By now you've picked, or been picked, or learned how to be nobody's. A man at the gym says something about it as if it were nothing: 'You can only stand in one place at a time.'

choices.label: Stand with the ones who took you in

outcomes.text: I stood with them. It's easy to look down on belonging, until you need it. It cost me what it cost. It gave me something to stand on.
I stood where I'd been put. A gang is a family you can't leave and don't pick. But it's a family.
I stood alone. It's a hard way. But there's a respect in it, among the old hands, for a man who asks nothing. I kept my back to the wall for years.
I stood alone. It was cold. But I had my own rules, and I knew them by heart, and no one else's name was on me.
I stood where the wind wasn't. It's cowardice and it's wisdom, and in this place they look the same. I was never hurt.
I played every side. It's an art. It cost me every friend I had, and kept me alive.

title: Something to hope for
text: It isn't a plan, exactly. It's the thing you do when the days have no shape: a course, a project, a letter, a scheme. You have found something, and it is yours, and you've begun to lean on it. An officer notices.

outcomes.text: I told the officer. He didn't laugh. He said, 'Good', and wrote down a name for me to ask. A door opened that I hadn't known was a door.
I told a friend, and he told another, and soon the whole landing knew. It became, in some small way, ours.
I kept it secret. It was mine. I took it out only in the dark and turned it over and over. It kept me alive.
I guarded it like a coal. A man who has nothing else needs one thing to be his. This was mine.
I took it as far as it would go. I wrote the letter, signed the form, joined the course. When the news came, I was a little less afraid.
I went all in. I told myself that hope was a discipline, and I practised it. It nearly broke me, and it saved me.

title: The test of the walls
text: It happens in an instant: the noise, the hands, the dark. When you come to, someone is kneeling next to you. 'You're all right,' he says. 'Stay down.' You are lying on the floor of the building. You are alive. It has tested you, and you have, for now, passed.

outcomes.text: I got up. I've got up since. It's the only thing the walls can't take, in the end.
I got up, shaking. The man who'd knelt next to me nodded. 'That's all it takes,' he said.
I stayed down. I breathed. The floor was cold, and the ceiling was a long way up, and I understood that I was lucky.
I lay there for twenty minutes. Nobody moved me. I think the ones around me knew what I was doing: I was learning to be alive again.
I wrote it down that night. I wrote every detail. I read it aloud, once, to a man on the landing. He said, 'You were lucky.' I said I knew.
I memorised it. I knew I'd need to tell it again, to a board, to a judge, to a child.

title: The door
text: There comes a day when the door seems nearer than the wall. It isn't a thing you can describe. It's a smell, a sound, the angle of the light on the landing. Something is about to change, one way or another. You can feel it in the building and in your own chest.

outcomes.text: I took every step as if it were glass. I kept my head down and my record clean. The nearer the door, the slower I went.
I walked toward it like a man crossing a frozen lake. Everyone does. The ones who run are the ones who fall.
I could not wait. I did something rash, on a Tuesday. It cost me a year, but I'd have done it a hundred times.
I took the risk. It was a mistake. It was also the only thing I've done in this place that felt like mine.
I didn't look. It's a technique. I did the days. I did the weeks. I did the years. When the door opened, I wasn't looking.
I kept my eyes on the floor. A friend told me, much later, that this is how most men do it.

title: Probation
text: A year. The probationary period ends with a signature and a handshake, in an office with a view of the car park. The deputy says, 'You'll do.' It's all the ceremony the job allows. He hands you a new, heavier ring of keys.

outcomes.text: I took them. They were heavier than I'd expected, in a way that had nothing to do with weight.
I took them. A small, cold thing, and a great deal of trust. I put them on my belt and felt the building take notice.

choices.label: Ask what the keys are for

outcomes.text: He laughed. 'Everything,' he said. 'Nothing. It's whatever you decide.' It's the truest thing anyone has said to me about the job.
He told me. He told me the cells, the stores, the gates. He didn't say what they open in a person.
I hesitated. It was a moment, no more. He saw it. 'Good,' he said. 'Keep that.' I've kept it.
I took a breath before I took them. The deputy nodded. 'I wouldn't trust anyone who didn't,' he said.

title: The first incident
text: You've been on the wing long enough to know that nothing is routine. This is the day it stops being theory. A man is down, or a door is jammed, or a voice is shouting your name. Everything you've been taught arrives in your hands.

outcomes.text: I did every step. It worked. Afterwards I filled in the forms with a hand that wouldn't stay still. It was the first time I truly understood what the training was for.
I followed the procedure. It's strange how a procedure can hold you up, like a rail.
I did what seemed right, and it worked, and I told no one how close it had been. I was commended for it. I've never been sure I deserved it.
I improvised, and the thing I'd done wasn't in the book. It turned out to be exactly right. I've been trying to explain it ever since.
I froze. For two seconds. It felt like two hours. A colleague pushed past me and did what I should have. We never spoke of it. It's the worst thing I've done, and the most useful.
I froze. The incident ended without me. I've been afraid ever since, of the next time, and I'm better for it.

title: What kind of officer
text: At some point, the building decides what you are. It does it without telling you. It notices what you do with the small decisions, the unrecorded ones. A colleague says it quietly, one night, over bad tea: 'You've got a reputation now.'

outcomes.text: He told me. It was both better and worse than I thought. Half the wing thought I was fair, and half thought I was soft. I could live with both.
He told me. It was different from what I'd hoped. But it was true, and truth is a kind of gift.
I leaned into it. I became, over time, what they said. It's a strange thing, to be shaped by a rumour.
I played the part. It was an easy one, and over time it became me.
I set out to be someone else. It took two years. I'm not sure I managed. But the effort did something to me, and not all of it bad.
I tried to change. The wing was suspicious. But eventually a few of them came round, and a few more didn't, and I stopped counting.

title: Stripes
text: The stripes arrive on a Tuesday. A sergeant now: forty officers on the roster, two hundred inmates on the landing and a radio that never leaves your ear. The deputy shakes your hand. 'Now it gets hard,' he says.

outcomes.text: I walked every landing in the first week, every shift. By the end of the month, I knew every name. They knew mine. A building is a lot easier to command when it's looking at you.
I led from the front. It exhausted me. But the officers followed.
I ran it from the control room. It was efficient. It was also remote, and in a year I'd lost touch with the wing. I regret that.
I delegated. It worked in the short term. In the long term I became a name on a door.
I asked the officers what they needed. They looked at me as if I'd grown another head. But they told me. And I listened.
I asked, and I was told. It wasn't what I expected. It made me a better sergeant than I would otherwise have been.

title: The long shift
text: You have been here a very long time. The recruits are younger than your children. The building has changed its paint twice, its policy three times and its name once. You walk the landing at night and find you know it better than you know your house.

outcomes.text: I stayed. I did my time on the other side of the door. When it was over, I understood something about the men I'd watched: that it's the same time.
I stayed to the end. It was the only decision I could imagine. It was, I think, the right one.
I put in my papers. It was a surprise to everyone, including me. The first morning I woke at 5.40 and lay there, listening for the keys.
I left. The building did not notice. It went on without me, as it will, as it always did.
I took a young officer under my wing and taught her everything I knew. When I finally left, she was ready.
I wrote it all down in a notebook and gave it to a recruit. Years later she wrote to say she still had it.

title: What came of it
text: Months after the hunger strike, the landing smells different. There are new vegetables in the kitchen, the roof has been patched, and a man in a good coat has been seen talking to the chaplain. Nobody mentions the strike, and everybody is thinking about it.

outcomes.text: I wrote up a list of the next three things that needed fixing. I gave it to the chaplain. He gave it to the man in the coat. The roof was done in the spring. The showers took another year.
I organised a petition. A hundred and sixty names. It was received without comment. A month later, there was a new rota for the laundry.
I let it be. Some victories are best left unpressed. The building held its breath, and nothing broke.
I kept my head down. It was a good year. They don't come often.
I let it be known that I had been at the heart of it. It was a lie. It got me a seat at a good table and a visit from a man I would rather not have met.
I let people think I was behind it. For a month I was somebody. Then someone who actually was walked into the mess hall, and the silence taught me a lesson.

title: The new arrivals
text: A new bus. Eleven of them, stumbling off in the grey light with their plastic bags. They're staring at the building as I stared at it. This time I'm the one at the window, with a mug of tea, watching.

outcomes.text: There was a lad, about nineteen, who held his bag in front of him like a shield. I stood next to him in the queue. Nobody touched him. At the end of the month he said, 'Why'd you do that?' I said I didn't know.
I looked after a quiet man with spectacles. He turned out to be a lawyer. He told me, within a month, three things about my case that nobody else had.
I stood in the corridor and asked for a light. I was the one doing it now. A young man gave me a perfect answer. I let him through, and felt both proud and sick.
I tested the newest. He cracked. I'm not proud of that. I've never forgotten his face.
I looked away. It's what the building does to you. I told myself it was nothing to do with me.
I looked away. The first few weeks are the worst, and I've no stomach left for them.

title: The date is set
text: It's been decided: the first Saturday after the lockdown lifts. The crew know. The man on the inside knows. In the small hours, in the dark, with the pipes ticking, you realise that there are now four people who could undo you.

outcomes.text: I moved it forward by a week. Nobody was ready. It put us ahead of whoever might have talked. I'm not sure it was wise. It was necessary.
I told them it was this Thursday. They looked at me, appalled. But they came. It was the best decision I've made, or the worst.
I called it off. The crew grumbled. Two of them thought I'd lost my nerve. A month later, one of them was caught with a length of cable. I'd been right.
I postponed it by a month. The feeling in my stomach didn't leave. But it didn't get worse.

choices.label: Test the inside man once more

outcomes.text: I tested him with a false date. Nothing happened on the night, no extra officers, no search. He was clean. I felt something in me settle.

intel: The inside man held a false date

outcomes.text: I tested him. He passed. I almost wished he hadn't.

title: What it cost
text: A year after you spoke up, the building has settled around the fact of it. There are people who won't sit near you in the canteen and a few who will. There is a letter on the noticeboard about a new complaints procedure, and your name is nowhere on it.

outcomes.text: I kept it down for a year. By the end of it the building had other things to be angry about. It's amazing how quickly the anger moves on.
I kept quiet. A younger officer thanked me, quietly, in the corridor. That was enough.
I put my name down. It surprised everyone, including me. I was elected by eleven votes. The first meeting was a tremendous argument, and I enjoyed it.
I ran. I didn't win. But I got two hundred votes, which was a good deal more than I'd expected.
I applied for a transfer to a training post. It was granted. I spent two years teaching recruits and never regretted a day of it.
I looked. There was a vacancy in another region. I didn't take it. But knowing I could made the difference.

title: The peace
text: It has been quiet on the landing for weeks. A kind of quiet that isn't peace, exactly. A man whom I once wrote up has stopped me in the corridor. 'I wanted to say,' he says, 'you were fair.'

outcomes.text: I said thank you. It was the only thing to say. We shook hands, which is against the rules. Neither of us mentioned it.
I thanked him. He walked on. I stood there for a minute, in the middle of the landing, with a lump in my throat.
I nodded, and said 'carry on'. He nodded, and carried on. We were two professionals, and it was a strange thing to be.
I said, 'Back to your cell.' He went. I felt like a clerk, and then I felt like a human, and then I went on with the shift.
He said, 'You never lied to me.' I thought about it all night. I couldn't remember the last time I'd told a lie to an inmate, and I was suddenly very proud of that.
He said, 'You looked at me when you spoke.' It's the simplest thing in the world, and I made a note.

title: The first meal
text: Nobody tells you how many decisions there are. A man behind a counter asks what you want, and what you want turns out to be a very large question. The menu has forty things on it. You've eaten from a tray for years.

outcomes.text: A cheeseburger, which tasted like grease and salt and a memory. I ate it slowly and thought it was the best thing I'd ever had, and also that something was missing, and the thing missing was the noise.
I ordered the thing I'd thought about for years. It was fine. The thinking had been better. I sat in the window and watched people walk past as though it was nothing.
I said 'whatever you're having'. The waitress smiled. It was the first time anybody had decided something for me kindly.
I let the person with me choose. I realised halfway through the meal that I was eating with my arm round the plate. I took it away, slowly.
It was too much: the light, the choice, the noise. I stood outside and breathed. Somebody asked if I was alright. I said yes, and meant it a little.
I walked out. I got a sandwich from a shop, in a bag, and ate it on a wall by myself. It was exactly what I needed, and I did not mind that nobody knew.

title: The phone
text: Everything is a screen. The bus has one, the bank has one, the form for the job has one and the form wants to know your email address, a thing you've never had. A teenager on the bus helps you without looking up.

outcomes.text: A boy of about twelve took it out of my hand, did it in four seconds and handed it back. 'It's easy,' he said, kindly. I thanked him far too much.
A woman at the library desk sat with me for an hour. She never asked why I didn't know. I have never forgotten it.
It took a week and a great deal of swearing. I got there. There was pride in it that was disproportionate to the achievement.
I got it wrong several times, including once in front of a queue. I went red. Then I got it right and nobody noticed.
I did without. It meant forms in person, queues, cash. It meant being the one with the paper. I got by, but the world is built for the other kind of person.
I kept to places that did not need it. It's a way to live. It's a narrow one.

title: The question on the form
text: It's the fifth interview. It's gone well. The manager likes you. Then the form comes out, and there's the box, and you know that however you answer, the room is going to change.

outcomes.text: I said it plainly: what, when, how long, and what I'd done with the time. He listened without writing. 'I'll be honest, that gives me pause. But the rest of what you've said doesn't.' I got the job.
I told him everything. He thanked me for my honesty and said they'd be in touch. They weren't. Honesty doesn't always pay, but I could look at myself.
'A conviction, a long time ago, served in full.' He nodded as though I'd said something about the weather. I took the job and carried that sentence home with me for weeks.
I gave the short version. It worked, once. Then a background check found the rest, and it looked much worse for the missing detail.
They didn't check. I started on Monday, and spent two years waiting for someone to look.
It came back to bite me. The HR woman was kind about it, which was worse. I was let go on a Friday with a box.

title: The deposit
text: The room is a decent one. The landlord is a tired man with a ring of keys. He wants a month's deposit, two references, and a look at your face while you say where you've been for the last few years.

outcomes.text: I counted out the cash and told him straight. He looked at the money for a long time. 'No trouble?' 'None.' 'Right,' he said, and held out a key.
I explained. He listened, then asked for six months' rent in advance. I paid it. It left me with very little, and a room.
My sister signed the form without a word and drove me to the door. She stood on the step until I had gone in, as though I might not.
I asked, and they said yes, and I had to carry that: the weight of someone else's name on my lease.
A friend's floor, a hostel, a car for two weeks in March. It's survivable. It's not a life, and I could feel the margin thinning.
I took what was offered by the day: a sofa here, a bed in a church hall there. People are kinder than they should have to be.

title: A very ordinary appointment
text: The probation officer's office has a pot plant and a poster about domestic safety. She has your file open and a look on her face that is neither friendly nor unfriendly. 'How's it going?' she asks.

outcomes.text: I told her about the money, about the temptation, about the man I'd seen. She wrote it down, calmly. 'That's what the appointment is for.' It was the first time I'd ever been helped by an official.
I told her it was hard. She didn't flinch. She sent me to a programme and a man who helps with CVs. It was a better conversation than I'd expected.
'All fine.' She nodded, and made a note, and there was a pause which told me she knew exactly what 'fine' was worth.
I said I was fine. I was not fine. She wrote 'doing well' and I walked out feeling worse than when I went in.
I didn't go. A letter arrived. Then another. I went to the next one, and she said, very gently, that there is only one more of those before it becomes something else.
I missed the appointment. The text from her said only 'please call.' It was the politest warning I have ever had.

title: The old crowd
text: Three of them are on the corner by the shop. They saw you before you saw them. One lifts a hand. They look older, and well, and there's a car in the road with the engine running that no one has mentioned.

outcomes.text: I crossed. It cost me a feeling in the stomach. But I didn't turn round, and that night I slept better than I had in months.
I crossed the road and kept my head down. One of them called my name. I did not look back. It's the loneliest thing I've done.
I stopped, shook hands, asked after somebody's mother. Nobody asked me for anything. I felt the pull of it all the same, like a tide.
We talked for ten minutes. One of them pressed a number into my hand, 'in case'. I put it in my pocket. I didn't throw it away.
I got in. It was, for a while, wonderful. It was familiar, and warm, and everything I'd missed. Six weeks later, it wasn't.
I got in. Nobody asked anything of me that night. Nobody had to.

title: The funeral you can attend
text: While you were inside, someone died. Now there's a grave, a stone, and a relative who says 'I'm sorry' and then, quietly, 'she asked for you'. The cemetery has gravel paths and a smell of cut grass.

outcomes.text: I stood at the stone for an hour. I said what I hadn't been able to say in letters. It didn't make anything right, but something in my chest unclenched a little.
I went at dawn, when the gates opened. I talked to the stone. A man cutting the grass pretended not to hear. I was grateful to him.
They didn't know what to say. We sat in the kitchen and said very little. My aunt gave me a photograph. It's on the shelf.
It was awkward and kind. A cousin asked how long I was out for, and nobody laughed, and then everyone did.
I couldn't. I stayed in my room that week with the blind down. I told myself I'd go next month.
I told myself it was too late to matter. I know that's not true. I think about it most days.

title: The child who remembers
text: She was six when you went in. She's tall now, with your jaw, and she looks at you across the table the way you'd look at a stranger who happened to know your name.

outcomes.text: I didn't push. I asked about school. She told me about a teacher. At the end she asked if I'd come to the school play. I said yes before she'd finished the sentence.
I let her decide the pace. Months passed. One Sunday she knocked on the door with her homework. Neither of us spoke about why.
She listened to all of it, white-faced. At the end she said 'I knew that.' She had known for years. We sat for a long time in the same silence.
I told her. She cried, and was angry, and then she asked a question I'd not expected: 'were you scared?' I said yes. It was the first honest conversation either of us had had.
I bought her a phone I could not afford. She thanked me politely. We both knew.
Presents. Cinema. A day out that tried too hard. She was kind about it. I understood afterwards that she didn't want things.

title: Being recognised
text: A woman at the checkout is looking at you in a certain way. Then she says, quietly, 'I know who you are. I read about it.' She isn't hostile. She isn't friendly. She is simply certain.

outcomes.text: 'That's right. I did the time. I'm doing something else now.' She nodded slowly. Her till beeped. 'Next,' she said, and the moment was over.
I told her it was true. She didn't say anything else. I went back to that shop for years. We never mentioned it again.
'You've got me confused with someone else.' She let it go, with a look. It sat in my stomach all day, the lie, and the knowledge that she knew.
I denied it, and left my shopping. I did not go to that shop again.
I put down the basket and walked out. In the street my hands shook. I had done nothing. That was precisely the point.
I paid, said nothing, and left. Later, I discovered she'd put a note in the bag. 'Good luck.' I still have it.

title: The first wage
text: It's in the account. It's real. It's not much, but it's earned, in a place with a time clock and a kettle and a man called Terry who nods at you every morning.

outcomes.text: I put away every spare penny. By the end of the year I'd saved a sum. It's not large, but it is a margin, and a margin is the difference between a bad month and a bad year.
I saved the lot, and bought nothing. My sister said I was being silly. I told her it felt like a wall.
I took them for a meal, and paid. My mother cried, quietly, into a napkin. I counted the cost and decided it was cheap.
I bought presents, and it felt like something. It was money well spent in a way no savings account can measure.
A weekend I can only partly remember. It was glorious. Then it was Monday, and it was nothing.
I spent it fast, on things I'd been thinking about for years. The pleasure faded faster than the debt.

title: A circle of chairs
text: A man from the programme leans against the door. 'There's a meeting on Thursday. Church hall. Tea, biscuits, no one will ask you anything you don't want to say.' He doesn't push. He's been where you are.

outcomes.text: Eleven people in a circle. A woman spoke about her brother. A man spoke about a car. I said nothing. On the way home I said something to myself, under my breath, that I'd never said before.
I went for the biscuits and stayed for the people. By the third week I was putting the chairs out.
I thought about it for a month. Then a bad night, and a phone call, and I turned up on a Thursday with my hands in my pockets.
I didn't go. He didn't ask again. The door stays open.
'I'm fine.' He nodded. 'Right.' He went off in a way that said he'd heard the words a thousand times and didn't believe a single one.
I said I managed. I did, mostly, for another two months.

title: What you were owed
text: A message comes through a cousin: someone from the old wing says there's a debt, and now that you're out, it's fair game. The amount is small. The tone isn't.

outcomes.text: I took the money to a pub and handed it over in an envelope. He weighed it in his hand and nodded. 'We're square.' We were. I think.
I paid it all. It left me thin for a month. But the message stopped.
I said no. Nothing happened for a month. Then a car followed me home. Then nothing again. You never know.
I said I'd done my time. It got back to him. He sent a note saying only 'we'll see', and every footstep behind me for a year sounded like him.
It felt like the thing I'd spent years learning not to do. But she took it seriously, and the problem went away without my name on it.
I told her. She wrote it up and made a call. A week later, a man was moved from one wing to another and that was the end of it.

title: Sleeping with the door open
text: You still wake at 5.40 for a count that doesn't come. You still sit with your back to the wall. You still can't sleep without the door closed and the light a certain way, and last night the sound of someone's key in a lock two flats away put you on the floor.

outcomes.text: A GP, twenty minutes, a leaflet. I said the word out loud. 'It's very common, in people who've been inside.' That was all. It was enough.
I told a counsellor everything about the nights. He didn't flinch. We built a list of small things that help. I use it still.
Routines, a light on in the hall, the radio low. It got easier slowly. It never fully stopped.
I got through it by being tired. I worked double shifts, so I'd sleep. It's not a solution.
A drink, then another. It worked, until it didn't. A year on, I was on the edge of something I knew the shape of.
I found something to take the edge off. It took the rest as well.

title: The apology that came with a cheque
text: A letter in an official envelope, and a second, thicker one from a solicitor. The state regrets the error. The state has calculated the regret to the nearest pound, and it is not as much as you would have chosen.

outcomes.text: The money didn't give back a day, but it made a deposit, and a business loan, and a second chance. I used it carefully, because I know what the absence of it feels like.
I took it, and put most of it away. The rest went on the things I'd waited years for. I don't regret any of it.
It took two more years. A lawyer, a hearing, a thin extra sum, and a statement that I could read aloud. It felt like winning something.
I took it to the end of the road and the end of the road was the same figure. But I'd said what I had to say, in a room, with the right people listening.
I gave most of it to the legal charity that had worked on my case. They looked at me as though they had not heard right.
I split it between a charity and a few people who had written to me. It felt like the only right thing to do with it.
